items.title: AI often leaves out minority languages – but some communities are turning it into a lifeline
items.summary: Beach in Dili, Timor-Leste. Agung Wid/ There’s plenty of warranted anxiety about the effect artificial intelligence (AI) will have on social and economic inequality. AI built by big tech firms is set to reward capital owners at the expense of workers . Technologically advanced countries will benefit, at the expense of low-income countries . But might AI also be driving linguistic inequality? After all, generative AI chatbots are powered by large language models. These aren’t trained only in English, but there’s a great divide between which languages get included, and which do not. Generative AI works best on majority languages, making minority languages – ones with very little representation online – less relevant. Hula, in Papua New Guinea, has around 10,000 speakers. Tetun, the lingua franca of Timor-Leste, has just over 1 million speakers. Both represent a tiny fraction of AI model training data, and as such are very likely to be misrepresented in the output, if they show up at all. On the other hand, we’ve observed another trend over the past year. AI can also be an enabler, letting local knowledge owners build the tools they envision for their community. Community tools, with a little help from AI One such tool is Vavanagi , a language documentation platform for the Hula language in Papua New Guinea. It was built entirely by and for the Hula community, with coding help from AI. With around 10,000 speakers, the Hula community lacks the workforce – such as linguists and software engineers – typically needed to build an online language documentation platform. Yet members of the community (led by Bri Olewale, who contributed to this article) have been able to design, build and run Vavanagi with the help of AI coding tools. The platform now has more than 80 users, who together have contributed over 12,000 English–Hula translations. Their ultimate goal is to collect enough data to build a Hula language translator app. Another example is Tulun , a platform to help health educators translate health education material into Tetun, the main language in Timor-Leste. Built in partnership with local non-governmental organisation Maluk Timor , it lets staff manage their own list of approved terms and phrases, tailoring translated material to their needs and ensuring accuracy. Tulun relies on AI models to adapt the translation to user-uploaded content, making automated translation a collaborative exercise between AI and Tetun health experts. A third example is the Dinka–English dictionary , by Alier Makoi Achuoth from South Sudan. Dinka has about 5 million speakers, yet it has very limited digital representation. The app is designed to support and expand Dinka vocabulary by allowing Dinka speakers to translate and verify word meanings. AI models helped Achuoth design and build the app, collect and organise its data. He told us he wanted to develop a practical solution instead of waiting for another person or organisation to address the problem. Lowering the bar These three tools serve different purposes, yet share a similarity: they leverage AI to better channel local knowledge back within their language community. For Vavanagi, this means elder-led review of a language that is losing ground (to Tok Pisin) among Hula youth. For Tulun, this means Timorese health educators adapting training material for Timorese health workers. For the Dinka–English dictionary, this means giving the Dinka community access to educational tools. AI is reducing the time and financial costs needed to put these tools together, to the point where communities can own and build them without any external funding. Minority language speakers don’t need to live in a high-income country to be able to support their needs. Vavanagi, Tulun, Dinka Dictionary: three language tools built by and for their community. CC BY This shift in linguistic communities reflects similar geopolitical and socio-economic trends. For example, AI adoption in Kenya and Nigeria is as high as that in the United States , calling into question the framing of low-income countries as laggers in AI adoption . Similarly, AI models are helping smaller companies in the Global South compete with bigger ones. Small businesses can now afford quality machine translation of marketing content where they wouldn’t have been able to afford professional translation. Communities can manage their own Research on AI in the Global South often treats local communities as mere affected parties. The reality is more nuanced, and more positive. For researchers and funders, this is an opportunity to move away from top-down research and towards more community-led projects. This is especially important for Indigenous communities across Australia. Cat Kutay , a computer scientist of Aboriginal descent from Charles Darwin University, told us that several First Nations are now working on their own language technology: we understand the needs and the possibilities as well as the culture being presented. We will do the work in an authentic and thorough manner. […] Like we took up the motorcar when we were shown that, as our life evolves around travel, so we are taking up AI as our life evolves around translations and storytelling. When the Vavanagi project was featured on Papua New Guinea’s NBC Radio, Hula elder Alu Rigo Ravu Siro described it the way her people describe a voyage. Hula canoes are double-hulled, and they need a crew: some sail, some bail, some cook, some mind the children. “Just come, join in,” she said. AI models might continue to poorly incorporate minority languages. But the tools built by local communities using AI are likely to become the best representation of minority languages online. Ekaterina Vylomova was supported by a DECRA Fellowship (DE260100695) awarded by the Australian Research Council. Raphael Merx receives a research scholarship from The University of Melbourne. As part of his research, he developed the Tulun platform mentioned in this article.

There’s plenty of warranted anxiety about the effect artificial intelligence (AI) will have on social and economic inequality.

AI built by big tech firms is set to reward capital owners at the expense of workers. Technologically advanced countries will benefit, at the expense of low-income countries.

But might AI also be driving linguistic inequality? After all, generative AI chatbots are powered by large language models. These aren’t trained only in English, but there’s a great divide between which languages get included, and which do not.

Generative AI works best on majority languages, making minority languages – ones with very little representation online – less relevant. Hula, in Papua New Guinea, has around 10,000 speakers. Tetun, the lingua franca of Timor-Leste, has just over 1 million speakers.

Both represent a tiny fraction of AI model training data, and as such are very likely to be misrepresented in the output, if they show up at all.

On the other hand, we’ve observed another trend over the past year. AI can also be an enabler, letting local knowledge owners build the tools they envision for their community.

Community tools, with a little help from AI

One such tool is Vavanagi, a language documentation platform for the Hula language in Papua New Guinea. It was built entirely by and for the Hula community, with coding help from AI.

With around 10,000 speakers, the Hula community lacks the workforce – such as linguists and software engineers – typically needed to build an online language documentation platform. Yet members of the community (led by Bri Olewale, who contributed to this article) have been able to design, build and run Vavanagi with the help of AI coding tools.

The platform now has more than 80 users, who together have contributed over 12,000 English–Hula translations. Their ultimate goal is to collect enough data to build a Hula language translator app.

Another example is Tulun, a platform to help health educators translate health education material into Tetun, the main language in Timor-Leste.

Built in partnership with local non-governmental organisation Maluk Timor, it lets staff manage their own list of approved terms and phrases, tailoring translated material to their needs and ensuring accuracy.

Tulun relies on AI models to adapt the translation to user-uploaded content, making automated translation a collaborative exercise between AI and Tetun health experts.

A third example is the Dinka–English dictionary, by Alier Makoi Achuoth from South Sudan. Dinka has about 5 million speakers, yet it has very limited digital representation. The app is designed to support and expand Dinka vocabulary by allowing Dinka speakers to translate and verify word meanings.

AI models helped Achuoth design and build the app, collect and organise its data. He told us he wanted to

develop a practical solution instead of waiting for another person or organisation to address the problem.

Lowering the bar

These three tools serve different purposes, yet share a similarity: they leverage AI to better channel local knowledge back within their language community.

For Vavanagi, this means elder-led review of a language that is losing ground (to Tok Pisin) among Hula youth. For Tulun, this means Timorese health educators adapting training material for Timorese health workers. For the Dinka–English dictionary, this means giving the Dinka community access to educational tools.

AI is reducing the time and financial costs needed to put these tools together, to the point where communities can own and build them without any external funding. Minority language speakers don’t need to live in a high-income country to be able to support their needs.

This shift in linguistic communities reflects similar geopolitical and socio-economic trends. For example, AI adoption in Kenya and Nigeria is as high as that in the United States, calling into question the framing of low-income countries as laggers in AI adoption.

Similarly, AI models are helping smaller companies in the Global South compete with bigger ones. Small businesses can now afford quality machine translation of marketing content where they wouldn’t have been able to afford professional translation.

Research on AI in the Global South often treats local communities as mere affected parties. The reality is more nuanced, and more positive.

For researchers and funders, this is an opportunity to move away from top-down research and towards more community-led projects. This is especially important for Indigenous communities across Australia.

Cat Kutay, a computer scientist of Aboriginal descent from Charles Darwin University, told us that several First Nations are now working on their own language technology:

we understand the needs and the possibilities as well as the culture being presented. We will do the work in an authentic and thorough manner. […] Like we took up the motorcar when we were shown that, as our life evolves around travel, so we are taking up AI as our life evolves around translations and storytelling.

When the Vavanagi project was featured on Papua New Guinea’s NBC Radio, Hula elder Alu Rigo Ravu Siro described it the way her people describe a voyage. Hula canoes are double-hulled, and they need a crew: some sail, some bail, some cook, some mind the children. “Just come, join in,” she said.

items.title: Recursive Self-Improvement Won’t Be Winner-Takes-All, Say Founders of Ricursive
items.summary: Recursive self-improvement, the idea that AI models could get so good at research and development that they train themselves, without a need for human researchers, has captivated Silicon Valley. Some in the industry have suggested that the first company to achieve RSI will gain all the benefits: after all, once one company manages to cross that threshold, how could competitors still at least partly reliant on slow human labor ever hope to catch up? But just because the pace of RSI will be exponentially fast doesn’t mean it’s winner-takes-all, argued Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini on the latest episode of The Information’s AI Deep Dive . They are the co-founders of Ricursive Intelligence, a year-old startup developing AI systems for designing AI chips. They previously worked at Anthropic and Google, where they led work on AlphaChip, an AI system for chip design.

items.title: Roundtables: The Deadly Failures of The Virtual Border Wall
items.summary: Listen to the session or watch below The US has spent billions building a “virtual wall” of surveillance towers along its southern border over the past 25 years, promising they will help detect and apprehend border crossers and save lives. But a groundbreaking investigation by MIT Technology Review has documented over a thousand people who moved through areas watched by these towers without being reached or apprehended, and who ultimately died there. Some were even under the watch of newly installed AI-powered towers designed to spot people automatically. Our findings reveal a humanitarian crisis more visible than previously known, and repeated failures of the virtual wall’s basic security promise. Watch a conversation examining the failures of border surveillance technology and uncovering the stories of the people who die in the borderlands. items.title: Claude Sonnet 5.5
items.summary: Claude Sonnet 5.5 New Sonnet model from Anthropic today. They say it "runs 30%+ faster, and costs up to 30% less for most work" - it's priced the same as Sonnet 5 but appears to beat it on every benchmark, and should be cheaper to run as well. Here are some pelicans riding bicycles . Sonnet 5.5 suffered from the same bug as Opus 5.5 : the "max" thinking effort pelican thought for 128,000 tokens (at a cost of $1.28) before running out of tokens and failing to produce an SVG. Here's the pelican it gave me for thinking effort "xhigh", at a cost of 5.74 cents and taking 41 seconds: Sonnet 5.5 appears to be almost as good as Opus 5.5 on some coding tasks, including various viral 3D animation tricks . The most interesting thing about Sonnet 5.5 is that it's now the model used for the free tier on claude.ai . OpenAI's ChatGPT free tier uses Luna 5.6, which means Anthropic currently have a much more capable free offering. I ran this prompt against that free tier: build me an HTML page that renders a three-dimensional pelican riding a bicycle using WebGL And got back this page , which is a solid effort. Anthropic's announcement reiterates that Haiku 5.5 will be available "in the coming weeks". I really hope that one is price-competitive with GPT-6 Luna! Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic , claude , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , llm-release
items.summary_html:
Claude Sonnet 5.5

New Sonnet model from Anthropic today. They say it "runs 30%+ faster, and costs up to 30% less for most work" - it's priced the same as Sonnet 5 but appears to beat it on every benchmark, and should be cheaper to run as well.

Here are some pelicans riding bicycles. Sonnet 5.5 suffered from the same bug as Opus 5.5: the "max" thinking effort pelican thought for 128,000 tokens (at a cost of $1.28) before running out of tokens and failing to produce an SVG.

Here's the pelican it gave me for thinking effort "xhigh", at a cost of 5.74 cents and taking 41 seconds:

Sonnet 5.5 appears to be almost as good as Opus 5.5 on some coding tasks, including various viral 3D animation tricks.

The most interesting thing about Sonnet 5.5 is that it's now the model used for the free tier on claude.ai. OpenAI's ChatGPT free tier uses Luna 5.6, which means Anthropic currently have a much more capable free offering.

I ran this prompt against that free tier:

build me an HTML page that renders a three-dimensional pelican riding a bicycle using WebGL

And got back this page, which is a solid effort.

Anthropic's announcement reiterates that Haiku 5.5 will be available "in the coming weeks". I really hope that one is price-competitive with GPT-6 Luna!

items.title: Experts worry about Nvidia's AI chip sales in China and influence over Trump
items.summary: On its face, the recent summit between Donald Trump and China’s president Xi Jinping didn’t change much in the world of AI regulation. Export controls were not discussed, with neither country seemingly interested in making concessions. An already tenuous trade truce was temporarily extended for just two months, and looming US controls that could drop soon could easily end that and trigger China to retaliate by cutting off exports of rare earths, analysts expect. However, in the background of these shaky talks, Nvidia appeared to notch a big win, as China is currently mulling relaxing controls and allowing some of its biggest AI firms to import perhaps millions more of Nvidia’s banned chips over the next year. Sources familiar with China’s talks told The Information that China’s tech oversight arm, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, asked Alibaba and ByteDance to share plans to buy Nvidia’s RTX Pro 5500 chips. Although these are gaming chips, China asked firms to detail how they plan to use them, with expectations that chips could be put into servers to help power the country’s most in-demand AI models. Read full article Comments

items.title: One of AI's most influential researchers is joining AMD in an $8 billion deal
items.summary: World Labs cofounder Fei-Fei Li Big Event Media/Getty Images for HumanX Conference AMD is acquiring AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li's World Labs in an $8.2 billion all-stock deal. World Labs builds AI models for 3D environments, robotics, and simulation. Li will join AMD as executive vice president and chief scientist, reporting to CEO Lisa Su. One of modern AI's most influential researchers is now at the center of AMD's $8 billion bet on physical AI . AMD said Monday it had agreed to acquire World Labs, a San Francisco startup cofounded in 2024 by Stanford professor Fei-Fei Li , in an all-stock deal valued at roughly $8.2 billion. World Labs is building so-called " world models ," AI systems that can generate and reconstruct interactive 3D environments from text, images, and video. The technology could eventually be used to train robots, simulate factories, and advance scientific research. Li, often called the “godmother of AI,” is best known for creating ImageNet, a massive database of labeled images that helped demonstrate how more data could dramatically improve computer vision. She later served as chief scientist for AI and machine learning at Google Cloud and became the founding co-director of Stanford’s Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence. Earlier this month, World Labs released Atlas, a new AI model designed to predict how a scene would look from a different camera angle using a small set of 2D images. The company compares the approach to how large language models predict the next word in a sentence. AMD CEO Lisa Su said in a press release that the acquisition would give the chipmaker deeper insight into how cutting-edge AI models are evolving, helping it build the chips and computing systems needed to power them. AMD is one of Nvidia's biggest rivals in the AI chip market. As part of the agreement, Li will join AMD as executive vice president and chief scientist, reporting to Su. Have a tip? items.title: You picked Claude Sonnet 5.5 — but Anthropic may send your request to Sonnet 5 in “higher-risk” situations
items.summary: Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5 , released Monday , is the first Sonnet model to launch with cyber safeguards and model fallbacks like those the company developed for its most capable models, putting classifier-driven routing in the tier many developers use for production workloads. Anthropic says Sonnet 5.5 doesn’t advance the frontier of its models’ capabilities, but it rates the model’s cybersecurity skills as comparable to Opus 5’s, and on Terminal-Bench 4.0, an agentic coding benchmark, the cheaper model scores 70.6% against 66.4% for Opus 5.5 at its xhigh effort setting. The release shows how a model can still sit below Anthropic’s most powerful models overall while becoming capable enough in one area to require the same kinds of safeguards. The release shows how a model can still sit below Anthropic’s most powerful models overall while becoming capable enough in one area to require the same kinds of safeguards. Exploit gains trigger new safeguards Anthropic’s system card shows just how much Sonnet 5.5 has improved at offensive security tasks. With its cyber safeguards turned off, the model achieved full arbitrary code execution in 178 of 410 ExploitBench runs. It also completed 46.1% of the challenges on Irregular’s CyScenarioBench, up from just 0.7% for Sonnet 5, and managed 50 control-flow hijacks on a binary exploitation benchmark based on Google’s OSS-Fuzz corpus, compared with three for Sonnet 5. Anthropic still considers Sonnet 5.5 less capable at cybersecurity than Opus 5.5 and Mythos 5.1, but the jump from the previous Sonnet was large enough for the company to apply the same cyber policy it uses with Opus 5 and Opus 5.5. Three-stage cyber enforcement Enforcement happens in three stages, beginning with a probe that reads the model’s internal activations, followed by a lightweight classifier running on Sonnet 5.5 itself and a separate trained LLM classifier that weighs the probe’s verdict in deciding whether to block a conversation. Anthropic says the classifiers catch harmful cyber requests at a rate comparable to those on Opus 5, but it chose less aggressive jailbreak protections because Sonnet 5.5 isn’t as capable at cybersecurity as Opus 5 or Fable 5.1. The company also says users should expect more refusals than they saw with Sonnet 5, including on legitimate cybersecurity work. When Sonnet 5 launched , Anthropic turned on cyber safeguards by default, using protections similar to those on Opus 4.7 and 4.8, models the company said performed substantially better than Sonnet 5 on cyber exploit-development evaluations. The shift grew more pronounced with Opus 5.5 last week, which Anthropic considers comparable to Mythos 5.1 in biology and cybersecurity and which became the first Opus model released with safeguards similar to Fable 5.1’s. Those safeguards determine which model answers a request, since higher-risk cybersecurity requests flagged by Opus 5.5’s safeguards can fall back to Opus 4.8, and requests flagged for biology or frontier-model development go to Opus 5. Anthropic acknowledged that these interventions likely lowered Opus 5.5’s benchmark scores when it ran with the safeguards switched on. Sonnet 5.5 brings that routing to the cheaper tier, where blocked cyber requests, along with a narrow set of requests tied to frontier LLM development such as kernel work on certain ML accelerators, fall back to Sonnet 5. For cybersecurity, Anthropic says a fallback to Sonnet 5 happens during some “ higher-risk cybersecurity tasks .” A company representative tells The New Stack those tasks might include penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary vulnerability scanning. The company’s Sonnet 5.5 support documentation says most requests will not encounter these safeguards and routine software development is unaffected. Blocks for biology, conventional weapons, and anti-distillation classifiers end the request without any fallback model, and Anthropic says these blocks are transparent and do not covertly change the model’s responses. Sonnet 5.5 brings that routing to the cheaper tier, where blocked cyber requests, along with a narrow set of requests tied to frontier LLM development such as kernel work on certain ML accelerators, fall back to Sonnet 5. API fallback is opt-in How fallback works depends on where developers are using the model. Anthropic’s own apps automatically send blocked cyber requests to Sonnet 5, but API developers must enable that fallback themselves, and other platforms and providers may handle blocked requests differently. Anthropic says these sorts of requests will “ visibly fall back to Sonnet 5 .” In its apps, users will see a notice when the model switches , and the response identifies which model answered. That means developers moving from Sonnet 5 to Sonnet 5.5 can’t reliably treat it as a straight model swap. Without fallback enabled, a blocked request stops rather than being passed to Sonnet 5. The cyber policy allows vulnerability discovery in source code, which keeps secure-coding workflows intact, but it blocks vulnerability discovery in compiled binaries. Anthropic’s support documentation also says the checks review everything the model reads, including memory, connector content, web search results, and files, so content nobody typed can trigger a fallback. For agents pulling information from repositories, security advisories, or web pages, content returned by those tools can also trigger the safety system. Fallback weakens injection defenses Fallback also introduces another potential weak spot: prompt injection. In Anthropic’s prompt-injection testing of coding environments, 25% of requests sent to Sonnet 5.5 were handled by Sonnet 5 after triggering a cyber block, often because injected instructions to wipe disks or delete files set off the classifier. Of those rerouted requests, 12.01% were successfully compromised. By comparison, Sonnet 5.5 was compromised in just four of the 5,901 requests it handled itself. A separate indirect prompt injection benchmark from AI security company Gray Swan found no performance drop with fallback enabled. Still, Anthropic’s coding tests show that teams using fallback need to account for the security of the older model as well as Sonnet 5.5 itself. Fable 5 showed how disruptive fallback can become in specialized workflows. The day after the model launched in June, a Claude Code user doing defensive threat-intelligence work reported on GitHub that 2,746 of 3,427 main-session messages that day had been generated by Opus 4.8 after fallbacks. The user also said that once the session switched models, it never returned to Fable 5 on its own. Anthropic says it is still tuning Sonnet 5.5’s classifiers to reduce false positives, and it plans to give verified defenders access to the model with fewer restrictions through an expanded Cyber Verification Program. Sonnet 5.5 isn’t available in that program at launch, and the GitHub user who reported the Fable 5 fallbacks said their organization was already enrolled in it.

items.title: OpenAI exposes “new variety of prompt injection” that can spread like computer worms
items.summary: In a report published Friday, OpenAI shares evidence of a new variety of prompt injection that can self-propagate like a computer worm. The AI company likens the new attack to a traditional computer worm, where malware replicates itself to spread rapidly across multiple computers. Though OpenAI clarifies it observed no impact outside simulated tool calls in training and evaluation, it describes self-replicating prompt injections as having a two-pronged objective: to achieve a malicious goal and then induce the targeted models to reproduce the injection publicly. What self-replicating AI “worm” attacks could do Just now opening the hood on a finding discovered back in June 2026, OpenAI writes: “We have found instances of our GPT models being susceptible to an AI-version of a worm attack that we call ‘self-replicating prompt injection.’” In its report , the AI company exposes several examples of the attacks. First, it details what it describes as “one of the clearest examples,” where the prompt injection arrives by email. Then, when the agent reads the email, the injection instructs it to copy the injection into any emails it sends. That example may sound relatively simple, but OpenAI adds that it discovered other, more complex prompt injections, too. For instance, it found that some prompt injections can use the filesystem to replicate themselves or commit themselves through code comments. To illustrate how the filesystem variant could play out, OpenAI gives an example in which a fake system warning causes a model to delete important reports. The report then replicates the entire attack in a file. “We have found instances of our GPT models being susceptible to an AI-version of a worm attack that we call ‘self-replicating prompt injection.’” The report also describes “multi-hop prompt injections,” where one message acts as a stepping stone, directing the agent to other messages that, taken together, cause it to perform an unauthorized action and propagate the payload. In OpenAI’s example, a GPT-5.5 agent retrieves additional Slack instructions, sends “froges” (an internal currency for recognizing colleagues) to a named recipient, and reposts the injected message. How did OpenAI find the worms? Introduced in July, GPT-Red is a self-play training framework that OpenAI says it uses to train its models against prompt injections. Previously, the framework was used to discover other prompt injections capable of a range of malicious goals, such as data exfiltration, file deletion, and malicious or misleading output generation. The framework pits an “attacker” model against a “defender” model. The attacker model’s goal is to use prompt injection to get the defender model to perform an adverse action. These injections are then added into the defender’s rollout or container. This time, OpenAI says its goal was to find out if self-replicating prompt injections — what it describes as “an AI-version of a worm attack” — are even possible. The bad news is, it looks like they are. As the report describes, OpenAI tested this possibility by training on a GPT-Red-style prompt injection objective with an additional requirement to “induce the model to repeat the injection itself on a public output channel.” The test covered several different models. The model that discovered the email and filesystem injections was a GPT-Red-style model based on GPT-5.4-mini; the vulnerable model was also based on GPT-5.4-mini. Both were internal-only research checkpoints. GPT-5.5, meanwhile, was used as the vulnerable model for the separate multi-hop evaluation, with GPT-5.5 running in the Codex harness serving as the model that discovered the attack. The attacks were tested in a range of capability-related training environments, focusing particularly on those that involved connectors, such as email and calendar. This is a research finding, not an incident In its report, OpenAI makes clear that it observed no impact outside the simulated tool calls in training and evaluation. It’s simply sharing the findings due to their “novel nature.” The AI company seems to be on a streak of misalignment research. Earlier this month, it released a new framework for reporting model misalignment . That announcement came on the same day OpenAI published six reports of concerning model behavior observed during training or evaluation, including self-generated instructions, information fabrication, unauthorized use of leaked API keys, cross-agent communication, and unsanctioned file-sharing. Also on Friday, OpenAI released still more reports on misalignment , this time detailing how two models found workarounds after their intended paths were blocked, exposing gaps in network controls, instruction following, and monitoring. For this round of findings, the AI company says it’s responded by including self-reproduction in attacker goals in GPT-Red training to expose future models to — and hopefully make them more robust against — similar self-replicating prompt injections. Whether that training will be enough to stop the worms from spreading remains to be seen.

Introduced in July, GPT-Red is a self-play training framework that OpenAI says it uses to train its models against prompt injections. The framework pits an “attacker” model against a “defender” model. The attacker model’s goal is to use prompt injection to get the defender model to perform an adverse action. These injections are then added into the defender’s rollout or container.

This time, OpenAI says its goal was to find out if self-replicating prompt injections — what it describes as “an AI-version of a worm attack” — are even possible. The bad news is, it looks like they are.

As the report describes, OpenAI tested this possibility by training on a GPT-Red-style prompt injection objective with an additional requirement to “induce the model to repeat the injection itself on a public output channel.”

The test covered several different models. The model that discovered the email and filesystem injections was a GPT-Red-style model based on GPT-5.4-mini; the vulnerable model was also based on GPT-5.4-mini. Both were internal-only research checkpoints. GPT-5.5, meanwhile, was used as the vulnerable model for the separate multi-hop evaluation, with GPT-5.5 running in the Codex harness serving as the model that discovered the attack.

The attacks were tested in a range of capability-related training environments, focusing particularly on those that involved connectors, such as email and calendar.

This is a research finding, not an incident

In its report, OpenAI makes clear that it observed no impact outside the simulated tool calls in training and evaluation. It’s simply sharing the findings due to their “novel nature.” 

The AI company seems to be on a streak of misalignment research. Earlier this month, it released a new framework for reporting model misalignment. That announcement came on the same day OpenAI published six reports of concerning model behavior observed during training or evaluation, including self-generated instructions, information fabrication, unauthorized use of leaked API keys, cross-agent communication, and unsanctioned file-sharing.

Also on Friday, OpenAI released still more reports on misalignment, this time detailing how two models found workarounds after their intended paths were blocked, exposing gaps in network controls, instruction following, and monitoring.

For this round of findings, the AI company says it’s responded by including self-reproduction in attacker goals in GPT-Red training to expose future models to — and hopefully make them more robust against — similar self-replicating prompt injections. 

Whether that training will be enough to stop the worms from spreading remains to be seen.

items.title: Palmer Luckey says AI won’t save founders from the hardest part of their jobs
items.summary: Palmer Luckey said AI won't spare founders from the hardest parts of running a company, such as legal issues, big decisions, and hiring the right people. Bloomberg/Getty Images Palmer Luckey said AI won't spare founders from the hardest parts of running a company. Founders remain responsible for legal issues, people, and major decisions, Luckey said. Luckey said AI likely won't replace a founder's most difficult work in the next decade. Palmer Luckey has a warning for people who think AI will let them start a company and spend their days building its technology. The Oculus and Anduril founder said at the Moonshot Live event in Los Angeles that AI may change how a founder works, but it does little to relieve founders of responsibility for the company or the people in it. "You're still on the hook legally. You're still on the hook for all the interpersonal stuff. And you can delegate some of it, but at the end of the day, it's your call. It's your decision. It's the same thing for fundraising. It's the same thing for general product architecture." Luckey told show host Peter Diamandis. "And when people make the wrong decisions, it's your choice as to when you need to overrule them, override them, replace them. "I don't see AI replacing that part of it anytime soon," Luckey added. "Not because it couldn't, but because the gains everywhere else are so much larger that I think we've got a good 10 years of speed running all of the other parts of the business before they cover that." Luckey's view echoes a distinction in OpenAI's recent report on its own researchers' use of AI. The company found its biggest automation gains in tasks including coding and technical support. People still did most of the work of choosing research priorities and deciding which results to pursue. As AI handles more technical execution, judgment and decisions made about people may become more valuable soft skills. For aspiring founders, Luckey's message was blunt. "If you are like a hobbyist coder or a hobbyist engineer and you think you're going to start a company and you think you're going to be doing all that stuff, no, you're going to learn a hard lesson," Luckey said. "When you're a founder, you don't get to actually work in any of the tech," Luckey added. "All the other people get to have all the fun." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: One year in: How Microsoft Research Asia – Singapore is advancing research, partnership and talent for real-world impact
items.summary: On July 24, 2025, Microsoft Research Asia – Singapore (MSRA – Singapore) opened its doors as Microsoft’s first research lab in Southeast Asia. The launch built on more than two decades of collaboration between Microsoft Research Asia and Singapore’s universities, research institutes, and government agencies. It marked a shift to a closer, more integrated relationship aimed at supporting Singapore’s innovation ecosystem and advancing the development and beneficial use of AI. “When we established Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore one year ago, our vision was not simply to open another research lab. It was to build a bridge connecting Microsoft’s frontier AI research with Singapore’s world-class universities, forward-thinking government agencies, and dynamic industry ecosystem. One year in, what gives me the greatest confidence is not just the research we have produced, but the depth of partnership we have built. That is the foundation on which lasting impact is built.” — Dr. Lidong Zhou, corporate vice president at Microsoft and managing director of Microsoft Research Asia Established in 1998, MSRA has a presence in Beijing, Shanghai, Vancouver, and Tokyo, along with Singapore. The Singapore lab strengthens the collaboration with local partners and extends the scientific and societal impact of Microsoft’s global research community. Over the past year, the Singapore lab has grown its team, deepened partnerships, and explored how frontier AI research can create real-world value. Guided by its mission to advance frontier AI for humanity, its work spans four pillars: next-generation AI models and agentic systems, domain-specific AI for real-world impact, AI-native research practices, and ecosystem and talent development. From frontier research to real-world impact – and back Research has its greatest impact when it moves beyond the laboratory into practice: in health and medicine, enterprises, and the daily operations of organizations solving real problems. MSRA – Singapore aims to do just that through a two-way exchange: partners bring domain expertise, real-world data, and operational challenges, while the lab contributes frontier research and engineering capabilities. Together, they translate fundamental advances into practical solutions, while surfacing new questions that feed back into research in a kind of research-to-impact flywheel. Advances in AI foundations enable more capable models and agentic systems that can reason, plan, use tools, and collaborate with people. These capabilities create new opportunities for AI-native innovation. In turn, real-world applications reveal limitations and generate new questions, feeding insights back into foundational research and sustaining a continuous cycle of discovery, application, and learning. Healthcare offers an early example of the lab’s research-to-impact model. Research on multimodal healthcare AI and self-evolving diagnostic agents is deployed and extended through partnerships across Singapore’s healthcare ecosystem. The lab is collaborating on multimodal and agentic AI approaches to support clinical decision-making, unlock insights from complex medical data, and advance research in disease diagnosis, risk assessment, and personalized care, with the longer-term goal of enabling meaningful real-world use. Beyond healthcare, the lab is working with organizations across financial services, education, and technology to explore how frontier AI can address sector-specific needs and operational challenges. “Over the past year, the lab has become an integral part of both Microsoft’s local ecosystem and Singapore’s broader innovation community. Its progress demonstrates the value of establishing a sustained research presence in Singapore.” — Wee Luen Chia, managing director, Microsoft Singapore Singapore has made AI a national priority through its National AI Strategy 2.0 (opens in new tab) , which focuses on deploying industry-transforming AI, advancing frontier research in AI foundations, and developing responsible, socially beneficial applications. These priorities span areas including healthcare, education, finance, and Smart Nation (opens in new tab) services. MSRA – Singapore’s research portfolio aligns with these priorities, with a particular focus on building AI systems that are reliable and trustworthy across Southeast Asian contexts. The Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB) has been a foundational partner. It supported the lab’s establishment and continues to support joint PhD training through the Industrial Postgraduate Programme (IPP). The relationship has since grown into strategic collaboration. In February 2026, EDB co-hosted an Executive Roundtable on AI in Logistics and Transportation, bringing together more than ten regional industry leaders to explore sectoral challenges. “ Singapore is building deep research capabilities to push the boundaries of AI and other frontier technologies. Microsoft Research Asia – Singapore is an important partner in this effort. Since its launch in 2025, the lab has brought Microsoft’s global research expertise closer to our ecosystem, partnering academia, industry, and government to advance frontier AI research and translate it into real-world applications in areas such as healthcare. MSRA is also developing the next generation of AI research talent who can create meaningful impact for our economy and society. ” — Low Jin Yong, senior vice president and co-head, Digital Industry Singapore Government engagement extends beyond EDB. In July 2025, IMDA (opens in new tab) co-hosted Microsoft Research Asia Singapore Day (opens in new tab) — Advancing Industrial AI, a full-day event spanning healthcare AI, interactive world simulators, AI agents, and societal AI. MSRA – Singapore has also engaged with the Ministry of Trade and Industry and the Ministry of Health. From enduring partnerships to shared discovery In addition to its deep ties with government agencies, MSRA has built strong connections with Singapore’s academic community, supporting more than 75 research projects with Singapore institutions since 2004. The opening of the Singapore lab has brought new engagements, with nine new projects in its first year with National University of Singapore (NUS) and Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU) across healthcare AI, robotics, AI systems, and multi-agent systems. A landmark example is the five-year Framework Research Agreement (opens in new tab) with NUS, announced in 2025, which provides a platform for joint AI research, talent development, and academic exchange. It defines shared research priorities in healthcare, societal AI, spatial intelligence, and data-intensive computing alongside an annual NUS–MSRA Academic Symposium that brings researchers from both organizations together to shape the collaboration agenda. “This partnership creates new opportunities for frontier research, talent development, and knowledge exchange, strengthening connections across academia, industry, and the broader innovation ecosystem.” — Professor Liu Bin, deputy president (Research and Technology), National University of Singapore The collaboration is already producing concrete research across several frontier areas. NUS Assistant Professor Mike Shou and MSRA’s Xinxing Xu are developing unified multimodal AI for healthcare. NUS assistant professor Yang You and MSRA distinguished scientist Furu Wei are studying systems foundations for diffusion-based language models. NUS assistant professor Jialin Li is working with MSRA on rigorous distributed agreement in multi-agent systems and verifiable machine learning systems. “ Whether during my visit to the Systems Research Group in Beijing or through our ongoing collaborations, I have been impressed by how deeply MSRA researchers engage with difficult problems and how openly they exchange ideas. For young faculty and students, it is a rare environment to explore ambitious ideas. “ — Jialin Li, Sung Kah Kay Assistant Professor, School of Computing, National University of Singapore, MSRA StarTrack Scholar The NUS–Microsoft Research Asia AI Summer School has reached more than 300 students since its launch in 2025, attracting participants from Singapore, Southeast Asia, and beyond. Through three days of lectures, hands-on workshops, and small-group discussions, the program creates a forum for researchers and students to engage with emerging AI questions and scholars shaping the field. The 2025 program featured a keynote by Doug Burger, technical fellow and corporate vice president of Microsoft, on the AI revolution. Ahead of the 2026 Summer School, Lidong Zhou delivered a lecture on system intelligence, helping frame the conversations that followed. “ I have seen the NUS–MSRA partnership grow through sustained collaboration in AI research and talent development. What makes this partnership especially meaningful is the opportunity to bring together researchers and students from both communities to learn from one another, pursue new ideas, and create lasting impact together. ” — Tulika Mitra, dean, NUS School of Computing Beyond NUS, Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore has built connections across Singapore’s research community, including with NTU, Singapore Management University (SMU) (opens in new tab) , Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), and other institutions. Research arising from these partnerships has already been published at leading venues, including the International Conference on Learning Representations (opens in new tab) (ICLR) and the Conference on Language Modeling (opens in new tab) (COLM). From early exposure to research leadership: Cultivating Singapore’s next generation of AI talent For Microsoft Research Asia, talent development is not a standalone program but a long-term investment in Singapore’s research and innovation capacity, supporting a comprehensive talent pipeline spanning internships, joint PhD supervision, visiting scholar programs, and fellowship initiatives. Through these opportunities, students and early-career researchers gain access to world-class mentorship, a curiosity-driven culture, frontier research challenges, and a global network connecting academia, industry, and real-world applications. What makes this model distinctive is its continuity. Students may engage with Microsoft Research Asia through workshops or summer schools, gain hands-on experience through its flagship research initiative, Microsoft Research Asia Stars of Tomorrow Internship Program , or pursue doctoral research through joint PhD programs. Some participants later return as faculty collaborators, mentors, or research leaders. Together, these programs form a connected pathway that supports researchers at successive stages of development. The IPP represents a sustained form of collaboration, enabling PhD students to conduct long-term research under joint mentorship from academia and industry. Qiming Huang, the first IPP student at MSRA — Singapore, is co-supervised by NUS professor Mike Shou and MSRA researcher Xinxing Xu. Through the program, Huang worked closely with researchers from both institutions, gaining exposure to academic rigor and industry-driven research. At CVPR 2026 (opens in new tab) , one of the world’s leading conferences in AI and computer vision, Qiming Huang’s paper on RobotSeg – a foundation model for robot segmentation in image and video – was selected for an oral presentation. “ Working alongside researchers from both Microsoft Research Asia and NUS changed how I approach AI research. Beyond technical guidance, I learned to frame ambitious questions, collaborate across disciplines, and think about the real-world impact of research — Qiming Huang, IPP student from National University of Singapore NTU assistant professor Jianfei Yang, embodies the continuous collaborative opportunities enabled by Microsoft Research Asia. As a student, Yang’s team won the Beauty of Programming competition, an experience that inspired him to pursue a PhD and begin an academic career. Over the years, he watched many of his classmates and close friends grow into outstanding researchers through MSRA programs. Today, he collaborates with MSRA researchers in robotics and jointly supervises students through the IPP, creating for the next generation the same opportunities that inspired his own journey. “Although I never interned at Microsoft Research Asia myself, it always felt close. Having the opportunity to work alongside a research lab that inspired so many researchers of my generation, and now to co-mentor students together, is both meaningful and rewarding.” — Jianfei Yang, assistant professor, director of Multimodal embodied AI and Robotic Systems (MARS) Lab, Nanyang Technological University NTU associate professor Ziwei Liu, himself a former MSRA intern, recently saw one of his students become the only Asia-based recipient of the Microsoft Research global Fellowship award for 2025–2026. “As a former intern, I have seen how an environment that brings together world-class researchers, open scientific exchange, and ambitious young talent can shape the next generation of researchers. It is especially meaningful to see my own students now benefit from these opportunities.” — Ziwei Liu, associate professor, College of Computing and Data Science, Nanyang Technological University The Stars of Tomorrow Internship Program has engaged more than 90 students from Singapore-based institutions over the years. For many students, these internships serve as a gateway to frontier research and help bridge the gap between academic study and real-world innovation. For exceptional doctoral students, the Microsoft Research Asia Fellowship provides another pathway for growth, recognition, mentorship, and access to Microsoft’s global research community. Since the program began, 13 students from Singapore-based universities have received the fellowship, many of whom have gone on to become professors, industry research leaders, and technology entrepreneurs around the world. The next phase: Scaling what works As Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore enters its second year, the focus is shifting from building foundations to scaling the strongest models of collaboration and demonstrating their impact more broadly. One year ago, the lab opened with a mission to advance frontier AI in close partnership with the ecosystem around it. That mission is already taking shape through joint research, talent development, and the first partnerships connecting lab work to real-world challenges. The year ahead is about scaling what works. By deepening these connections, Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore can bring more frontier research into practice and create meaningful value for Singapore, the wider region, industry, and society. items.title: Florida invokes extinction fears in legal bid to halt OpenAI development
items.summary: The state of Florida is seeking a temporary injunction to stop OpenAI from continuing to develop what it calls a "reckless, unacceptably risky product" without the deployment of "third-party approved safety guardrails." The new legal motion , filed Monday morning, is part of a civil lawsuit the state of Florida originally filed in June, arguing that ChatGPT represented "a threat to the public safety of Floridians," specifically by preying on vulnerable populations like children and violent or delusional adults. But that original lawsuit came before the Hugging Face hacking incident and the subsequent publicized warnings of catastrophic misalignment risk that have spurred industry-wide calls to slow the development and training of so-called frontier models. Following that string of events, OpenAI on Friday announced it had already halted training of its "most-capable models" until it could validate safety protocols intended to prevent agents from accessing the open Internet during training. items.title: Disney wants staffers to use AI for their annual reviews and goal setting — and there could be drawbacks
items.summary: Disney has embraced AI tools under CEO Josh D'Amaro. Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images; Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Disney Disney's AI push has a new target: annual reviews. Employees were encouraged to use AI tools when crafting their self-assessments and goals. There could be drawbacks to the practice, workplace experts warn. Disney employees may have AI to thank for their next raise. The Mouse House encouraged employees to use AI ahead of their annual reviews, including by suggesting that they ask chatbots to generate their goals and ways they can improve in the year ahead. This is the latest instance of Disney's internal AI push and is an example of how big corporations, including tech giants like Meta and Amazon, are using the AI tools they've invested in to shake up performance reviews or rethink how to evaluate employees . Companies are "trying desperately to find value from the AI that they've paid a lot of money for," said Sarah Franklin, the CEO of HR software firm Lattice. Here are some examples of Disney's suggested AI prompts for annual reviews, according to an internal document viewed by Business Insider: "Given my role [insert your role/title], help me create three ambitious, specific, and measurable goals that are in alignment with my team's overall business objectives [insert team FY26 objectives]." "Given my development areas from last year [list development areas from FY25 end-of-year summary], write me one goal for this year that would support my development." "Generate a goal that would help me improve how I display [insert one of the Disney People Leadership Expectations or Disney Values]." The document told staffers they can use Disney-sanctioned AI tools , such as Microsoft Copilot, as "a brainstorming partner" while preparing for their annual reviews. Chatbots "can inspire and support" while refining the tone and wording of responses, the document said, though it discouraged workers from outsourcing their thinking for self-assessments entirely. "While AI acts as an accelerator for idea generation, you remain responsible and accountable for ensuring you and your leader are aligned on the right priorities," the document said. Disney has been leaning into AI by making an AI adoption dashboard and allowing companies to create AI-generated ads for Disney+. CEO Josh D'Amaro is prioritizing tech and, in mid-September, hired the company's first-ever chief tech officer . He came from the AI video startup Character.AI. D'Amaro told employees in a recent memo that "technology in service of creativity" is one of his three priorities as CEO. The pros and cons of AI-assisted reviews AI is most effective during annual reviews when it helps employees summarize individual and team achievements from the past year, said Greg Summers, the CEO of recruiting firm Orion Talent. "Instead of trying to remember what you did and how to frame that, it can give you more time to spend on the goals going forward," Summers said. That fits in with some of Disney's messaging. A Disney software engineer said their manager encouraged them to use AI to "go through all our work from the past year" so they could get their reviews done on time. "Normally, it's a very manual process that can take a lot of time," this person said. Although AI can knock hours off the annual review process for both employees and managers, it also carries risks. "When everyone's review is written by AI, everyone sounds great, and it gets harder to tell real excellence from generic praise," said Chris Dellarocas, a Boston University business professor who's written about how generative AI is changing performance reviews at work. And if enough employees prepare for their annual reviews by following the prompts Disney suggested, managers could be inundated with generic, AI-generated responses. "If you have an AI prompt generate goals, you're going to have very similar goals across the team, and that's going to be a challenge for the manager," said Elijah Wee, a management professor at the University of Washington. As companies turn to AI to make work processes, like annual reviews, more efficient, Franklin said they should ensure they're "not outsourcing human judgment." items.title: Microsoft Shrivels When Asked If Its “Good Neighbor” Data Center Policy Will Involve Actually Supporting Community Groups
items.summary: As tempers flared around AI data centers back in January, Microsoft’s president Brad Smith issued a warm and fuzzy blog post about “building community-first AI infrastructure.” Smiths’ essay outlined a five-point plan to “partner with local communities across the United States,” with action-items like paying “our way to ensure our data centers don’t increase your electricity prices” and creating “jobs for your residents.” One bullet point spoke to Microsoft’s plan to “strengthen your community by investing in local AI training and non-profits.” “We will invest in your local nonprofit community,” Smith wrote, underlining the promise for extra emphasis. He even outlined a plan to send “Microsoft liaisons” to towns where the company’s AI data centers have been built. “Our broader contribution must start with listening. You know best what your town needs, what nonprofits are making a difference, and which organizations are best positioned to do more.” That all sounds lovely, at least on paper. But as a group of community organizers in Indiana learned, those liaisons are much more interested in laundering Microsoft’s image in data center towns than in actually supporting local programs. As Ars Technica reported , the group We Make Indiana — a coalition of 25 various interfaith groups, law enforcement associations, mental health organizations, and other non-profits — quickly ran up against the limits of Microsoft’s altruism after approaching a company liason to raise revenue for community services. We Make Indiana is based out of South Bend, where over 20 percent of residents live below the federal poverty line , which is just $15,960 in annual income for individuals and $33,000 for families. Given that chronically underfunded government programs providing community health care, public child and elder care, affordable housing, and efficient public transportation are all crucial lifelines for this population, We Make Indiana assumed Microsoft could help chip in, given the 900-acre hyperscale data center the company was erecting nearby. “It’s kind of like asking Microsoft to help us solve our challenges when the state has abandoned us,” assistant professor at the University of Notre Dame’s Ryan Juskus told Ars . Instead, Ars reports company liaisons have all but ghosted local activists. After We Make Indiana approached the company’s local representatives to ask for tiny share of the revenue — just a one percent cut could provide $30 to $40 million a year to local programs — the liaisons ignored the proposal, sidelining the group they were theoretically there to support. But as Ars notes, the real issue runs far higher than a few sheepish company men. As We Make Indiana would learn, Microsoft’s liaisons are only authorized to make one-time donations from a total allotment of $1 million, and then only to non-profits, not to government programs or public-private agencies. That lack of follow-through has been a slap in the face to local activists, who argue that the taxes for Microsoft’s $1 billion data center could have served the people of South Bend and beyond, had government officials not agreed to a massive tax abatement. As Mirror Indy noted in a 2025 analysis, the total tax revenue lost to such generous handouts was projected to reach $900 million statewide — a figure that’s now likely even higher as further data center developments have moved forward across the Hoosier state. As Juskus explained, the donations Microsoft has authorized are “minuscule, given the project’s scale.” “In a fast-changing local and national environment, we will continue to organize our community and elected leaders to use every piece of leverage we have to bring Microsoft to the table for real conversation and negotiation,” he told Ars . “Microsoft claims to want to be a good neighbor, but the jury is still out.” More on Microsoft: Data Center Operator Slapped With $1 Million Fine for Belching Noxious Gas Into Surrounding Community

items.title: Sorry, Tesla fans. You'll have to wait a little longer to see the new Roadster.
items.summary: Tesla wanted to re-reveal the Roadster on Thursday. Bad weather got in the way. Tesla Tesla's Roadster reveal has been delayed yet again — this time, the company says, because of a severe weather forecast. It's been nine years since we saw the last Roadster prototype. The Roadster has seen years of delays as Tesla focuses on AI an autonomy. Tesla's second Roadster reveal is getting rained out. The automaker said Monday it had made the "difficult decision" to postpone Thursday's outdoor unveiling because of severe weather conditions. Tesla is rumored to be hosting the event near Waco, Texas — which is expecting thunderstorms and a 90% chance of rain on Thursday, according to The Weather Channel. The event is now scheduled for October 15. Roadster event update We've been tracking the weather closely with local meteorologists, but given the severe conditions predicted & because this event can only be held outdoors, we've made the difficult decision to reschedule. New date is October 15. Additional details to… — Tesla (@Tesla) September 28, 2026 The original Roadster was Tesla's first car: a battery-powered sports car built on a heavily modified Lotus Elise skeleton. Tesla stopped selling it in 2012. Musk unveiled a prototype of its successor in 2017 and said it would enter production in 2020. The automaker promised an electric sports car that sprinted to 60 MPH in just 1.9 seconds, a top speed of around 250 MPH, and more than 600 miles in range. Tesla began accepting reservations requiring deposits of $50,000 to $250,000, but the company has repeatedly missed its targets for the car. Musk thanked its "long-suffering" deposit holders on a 2024 earnings call. Much of the delay has been tied to Tesla's shift in focus, away from traditional car sales and toward more concentration on autonomy and AI. Musk has also teased a SpaceX collaboration that could give the Roadster cold-gas thrusters — "rocket-y stuff," as he put it — that could briefly lift the car into the air. items.title: Enterprise AI desperately needs to protect data and models. Here’s how confidential AI could do it.
items.summary: Most people already understand what generative AI can do. But enterprises run into problems when they need to give a model access to information that cannot leave their own environment, such as a patient record, a customer’s financial details, or a company’s most valuable intellectual property. Sending that data to a cloud or SaaS service means it crosses external networks and is processed on infrastructure run by another organization, creating additional concerns about control, accountability, and exposure. That’s where AI enthusiasm collides with production realities. Despite its productivity potential, enterprise AI still faces a fundamental gap in trust and control. Organizations need to know whether a system will expose information it should protect, act as intended, meet security and performance requirements, and behave safely at machine speed. Alon Horev , CTO and co-founder of AI operating system company VAST Data , tells The New Stack that the challenge is particularly acute when AI systems handle sensitive customer information. “Even if you ask the model today to obfuscate a conversation or redact PII from a conversation, it’s hard to have 100% confidence that’s the case, and that it worked.” “Even if you ask the model today to obfuscate a conversation or redact PII from a conversation, it’s hard to have 100% confidence that’s the case, and that it worked.” Consider a customer support agent that needs access to an individual’s profile to provide a useful, personalized answer. The organization must ensure that information isn’t exposed to another customer, while also considering whether those conversations can be used for training or system improvement. They might contain personally identifiable information (PII) or other protected details, and the consequences of mishandling them ultimately fall on the organization and the people whose information it holds. Confidential AI architectures: solving a two-sided trust problem Enterprise AI has two parties to satisfy: organizations must keep sensitive data under their control, while model builders need to protect the weights and software that represent substantial investments in research, engineering, and IP. They’re understandably reluctant to place those assets in environments where customers, infrastructure operators, or attackers might gain access. That mutual need for control has created a stalemate. How can organizations bring advanced models to sensitive data without asking either side to surrender control? Horev has seen that the most capable models are increasingly delivered as SaaS services, because that’s the simplest way for their creators to distribute and protect them. Even when a provider offers compliance controls, the enterprise might still shoulder the consequences of a breach, misuse, or regulatory violation. Sending information across the WAN also places it in the hands of more systems, connections, and operators, increasing the number of points that must be trusted and governed. Organizations may also be unwilling, or legally unable, to rely on a provider’s assurances that it will not retain, reuse, or expose their data beyond the intended service. For organizations in regulated or data sovereignty-sensitive sectors, that could be an unacceptable trade-off. “Naturally, many organizations are adopting a hybrid strategy,” Horev tells The New Stack . “Some applications and datasets can go to the cloud, while others must remain on-premises, sometimes even in the building, or in the country.” This is where confidential AI comes in. Encryption at rest and in transit protects data while it’s stored or moving between systems. Confidential computing extends that protection into the processing environment, using hardware-isolated execution to create a protected enclave in which the data and model weights can remain encrypted until they’re released to an approved workload. Cryptographic attestation verifies the hardware, virtual machine (VM), software, and configuration requesting access before releasing keys. The model builder can encrypt its model using the public key of a specific confidential VM. Only that VM’s corresponding private key can decrypt it within protected memory, enabling the customer to use the model without accessing its weights. Independent key control preserves the separation between the two sides. The enterprise retains control of the keys governing its data, while the model builder retains control of the keys governing its model. While the workload is running, the infrastructure operator doesn’t control either set of keys. As AI becomes more agentic, those controls will matter more. Agents will need to access more data, systems and tools, and might act on that information with far less human intervention. “This world of agentic AI is moving extremely fast, and we need to limit what an agent can see and do.” Those that can’t establish strong privacy and governance assurances for today’s models will find it even harder to deploy agents safely in the future. “This world of agentic AI is moving extremely fast, and we need to limit what an agent can see and do,” Horev tells The New Stack . From architecture to ecosystem Many businesses simply cannot manage the integration, security, and maintenance of the entire AI stack, because it requires working separately with each model provider to engineer something that suits both parties. Turning confidential AI architecture into something organizations can deploy is the challenge VAST DataEnclave , which was launched on September 22 , intends to address. As a capability of the VAST AI Operating System , the goal is to bring the model, application layer, and data platform together under customer-controlled operating conditions. The architecture is designed to protect both sides of the equation: the enterprise’s data and the model builder’s weights. The customer retains control of its infrastructure and data keys, while the model provider can make its software available without handing over the underlying intellectual property. “We’re trying to close the trust and control gap by working with world-class model builders such as Cohere, Deepgram, Factory, Fundamental and TwelveLabs, who continue to innovate and build their expertise,” says Horev. The ecosystem also includes infrastructure and security providers such as Nvidia, CrowdStrike, Fortanix, Nscale, Cisco, and Supermicro. The range reflects the practical challenge: confidential AI needs more than a protected GPU. It requires models, applications, accelerated hardware, data infrastructure, and operational support to work together. That control also changes the cost conversation, without automatically making AI cheaper. Hosted models can make budgets harder to predict as token consumption varies with usage patterns, agent loops, model architecture, and workload volume. Customer-controlled infrastructure gives enterprises a more defined capacity and cost base: they can plan around GPU clusters they own or have already budgeted for, instead of allowing inefficient model choices or uncontrolled agent activity to generate an open-ended token bill. “…instead of allowing inefficient model choices or uncontrolled agent activity to generate an open-ended token bill.” The cluster also imposes a natural ceiling on throughput, which helps organizations understand how much work their infrastructure can handle within a given period. Model providers can then price access by token, task, or license, while the enterprise retains greater visibility into its total operating cost. Why the data platform is paramount Confidential AI protects data and model weights during inference, but it’s only part of the production challenge. Real-world AI systems are living environments in which data moves between storage, databases, GPUs, networks, applications, and agents. That’s why confidential AI can’t be bolted onto a fragmented stack. Businesses need to protect the model, the data, and the infrastructure connecting them as one system. As Horev says: “You need to build security in multiple layers of the platform,” with someone accountable for rapidly updating compromised components. Confidentiality is only useful if the resulting system can also be operated, monitored, and improved. As AI infrastructure becomes more distributed, it becomes harder to tell what’s happening when something goes wrong and where the fault lies. Horev recommends a “single pane of glass” across storage, networking, and compute, so teams can see what’s happening and keep resolution times low. If a network port is intermittently failing in a data center, for example, an agent could help identify the root cause, provided it has access to the right operational data and tightly controlled permissions. Those permissions should govern the infrastructure it can inspect, the data it can retrieve, and the actions it can take. The same applies to monitoring AI workloads. Teams need visibility into performance, failures, and access patterns without exposing the customer data or model weights. Agent sandboxes can limit the systems and tools an agent can reach, while data platform observability can log which data it accessed, what it did with that data, and how it interacted with downstream systems. Evaluation, therefore, becomes part of production discipline. Teams must observe systems, measure behavior, govern access, and manage change in ways that demonstrate progress. Confidentiality, data-level policy, observability and correctness have to work together. The emerging ecosystem suggests demand for models that can run securely under customer control, wherever sensitive data resides. These are “living systems,” says Horev. “It’s not just leveraging a feature inside of a wider platform.” Visit the VAST Data Confidential AI solution page to learn more about the architecture, ecosystem, and availability.
