items.title: Anthropic bought Stainless and shuttered its SDK generator. Cloudflare open-sourced Forge instead.
items.summary: Cloudflare has announced an open source tool that takes an API definition and automatically produces the SDKs, command-line tools, documentation, and other interfaces used to interact with it. Forge, as it’s called, is available under an Apache 2.0 license , and can be run and modified privately without paying Cloudflare a dime. In a blog post published on Monday by Dimitri Mitropoulos , Matt Taylor , and Samuel MacLeod , Cloudflare notes that the project is still early: it already generates the output required for Cloudflare’s cf CLI , its unified command-line interface for working across the Cloudflare platform, with the company’s API documentation and SDKs due to move over in the coming months. “We believe that building tools for APIs is a core part of the Internet, and you should be able to do that without needing a SaaS product.” “We believe that building tools for APIs is a core part of the Internet, and you should be able to do that without needing a SaaS product,” the authors write. When your SDK generator disappears Cloudflare’s announcement comes just 11 days after Google made a somewhat similar move, revealing it had partnered with API tooling company Speakeasy to open-source the latter’s OpenAPI code-generation suite under an AGPLv3 license. In a blog post published September 17, Google said its decision was prompted by the sudden loss of its SDK-generation service, after the provider was acquired and “abruptly announced its shutdown.” This happened just as Google was preparing to launch a new API. “This sudden disruption highlighted that proprietary, closed-source generators create unacceptable platform risk.” “This sudden disruption highlighted that proprietary, closed-source generators create unacceptable platform risk,” the company wrote. “If the industry relies on OpenAPI to define interfaces, the tooling to compile those interfaces into client libraries, CLIs, and agent tools should be open infrastructure.” The provider Google was referring to was Stainless . Anthropic acquired the SDK and MCP tooling company on May 18, after which Stainless said it would wind down its products, including the SDK generator used to keep client libraries updated as APIs changed. As The New Stack reported at the time , the closure affected a swathe of customers including OpenAI, Google and Cloudflare. While those companies retained the SDKs Stainless had already generated for them, they lost the shared service they had relied on to regenerate and update those SDKs as their APIs evolved. Cloudflare, for its part, had already begun building some of the machinery that would become Forge. In April, the company released a technical preview of cf, a new unified command-line interface intended to eventually expose Cloudflare’s products through a consistent set of commands for developers and AI agents. At the time, Cloudflare said it had created a new TypeScript-based schema and generation system to keep CLI commands, configuration, bindings and other interfaces in sync with its API. That earlier preview was limited, but cf has now entered open beta with support across Cloudflare’s API. Forge reads the OpenAPI descriptions Cloudflare already maintains for its products and uses them to create cf’s commands, allowing the company to expand from roughly 280 functions in Wrangler to more than 3,000 operations across Cloudflare’s API. Cloudflare intends cf to replace Wrangler: once the beta ends, it plans one final major Wrangler release before moving the older tool into maintenance support for 18 months. Cloudflare, it’s worth noting, is pitching cf particularly heavily at AI agents: a single CLI can now be used to do things such as deploy and monitor a Worker, configure Cloudflare Access, buy a domain or manage WAF protection. It also defaults to JSON output and includes a natural-language command search intended to help agents find the right operation without loading thousands of possible commands into context. And this is also a useful illustration of what Forge is for. Rather than maintaining SDKs, CLI commands and documentation as separate implementations, Cloudflare can generate them from the same underlying API definition. As that API changes, the corresponding developer — or agent — interfaces can be regenerated from the same source, reducing the amount of hand-maintained tooling that has to stay in sync. Why Cloudflare built its own generator While Stainless was one of the hosted generation products Cloudflare had relied on in production, Cloudflare doesn’t name it specifically, instead spelling out why Cloudflare had become dissatisfied with the broader category of hosted generators. Part of the problem is sheer volume: Cloudflare says it now has more than 3,500 API operations, backed by hundreds of services maintained by different engineering teams. A generator therefore has to keep changes across that sprawling API estate accurately reflected in the tools customers use, without turning every update into a coordination exercise across the company. Cloudflare also wanted engineers to see what an API change would do to the resulting SDK, CLI and documentation before the underlying code was merged. Moreover, it wanted the same system to reach beyond conventional SDKs into things such as MCP servers and Cap’n Web bindings, which allow applications to invoke remote services through Cloudflare’s TypeScript-based RPC system in much the same way they would call local functions. That had proved difficult with external services. Cloudflare says problems introduced in one part of its API could surface only when another team later tried to release something, leaving engineers to trace the failure back through systems they did not fully control and then coordinate a fix across company and vendor boundaries. “We’ve tried several hosted products that attempt to solve this, and relied on some in production,” the authors write. “None of them solved this problem for us, and some have shut down entirely.” The open-source factor And so the Stainless wind-down goes some way toward explaining why Cloudflare is making Forge open source. Stainless’s generator was proprietary and delivered as a hosted service, leaving customers dependent on the company continuing to operate it. Forge’s permissive Apache 2.0 license means developers can run it on their own infrastructure, modify it, or fork the project and continue using it independently of Cloudflare. AI agents raise the stakes further, because they increasingly rely on SDKs, CLIs and API bindings to understand what software can do and how to interact with it. If those interfaces lag behind the underlying service, the agent may be working from an incomplete or outdated description of its capabilities. That is the concern Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht highlights when explaining why keeping those interfaces current matters more than ever today. “APIs have always been how software connects, but AI agents make the quality of SDKs, CLIs, and API bindings even more important,” Knecht tells The New Stack over email. “If that layer is stale or incomplete, an agent doesn’t just have a worse developer experience, it can misunderstand what a service can do.” Ultimately, Cloudflare created Forge because SDK and CLI generation has “become too important” to sit outside its internal development process. “Cloudflare needed a pipeline our teams could run, test, and extend themselves, and we think other developers should have access to that same kind of open, vendor independent foundation,” Knecht says. Forge still has plenty to prove, of course. The project is early, cf is its first production output, and Cloudflare says its API documentation and existing SDKs will move over during the coming months. Several of the input formats and generated targets it discusses are also future work. But the timing is quite revealing. Within 11 days, Google and Cloudflare — both former Stainless customers — have publicly thrown their heft behind open source SDK-generation infrastructure after the disappearance of the proprietary service they had relied on. Google describes that dependency as an “unacceptable platform risk.” Cloudflare, with Forge, is now trying to remove the same risk from its own stack.

items.title: The End of Privacy Is Here (with Kashmir Hill)
items.summary: Facial recognition is everywhere now. It’s in surveillance cameras; it’s soon going to be in Meta’s RayBan pervert glasses, and some students already did that. You now have massively viral accounts that take clips of people, run them through facial recognition software, and then post their name and other personal info for everyone to see. We haven’t fully come to terms with what it means to live in a world where anyone can basically dox anyone else now. To talk through this, Joseph spoke to Kashmir Hill. She’s a reporter at the New York Times, and the author of ⁠Your Face Belongs to Us: A Tale of AI, a Secretive Startup, and the End of Privacy⁠ . Facial recognition is everywhere now. It’s in surveillance cameras; it’s soon going to be in Meta’s RayBan pervert glasses, and some students already did that. You now have massively viral accounts that take clips of people, run them through facial recognition software, and then post their name and other personal info for everyone to see. We haven’t fully come to terms with what it means to live in a world where anyone can basically dox anyone else now.

To talk through this, Joseph spoke to Kashmir Hill. She’s a reporter at the New York Times, and the author of ⁠Your Face Belongs to Us: A Tale of AI, a Secretive Startup, and the End of Privacy⁠.

items.title: Humans Are Reading Copilot Prompts — And They're Horrified
items.summary: This piece contains references to eating disorders. If you or someone you know needs help, support is available . Human contractors hired to improve Microsoft’s Copilot AI chatbot are constantly bombarded with lewd or sexually explicit photo editing requests and images that users have uploaded, including upskirt photos or putting women into sexual positions. These contractors are then asked to review whether the generated image successfully fulfilled the prompt — such as, did the image generator make the woman’s AI-enlarged breasts big enough. When a Copilot user uploads a picture of themselves or someone else, they probably expect that image to remain private between just them and the AI tool. In reality, a workforce of at least hundreds of human reviewers are sometimes looking at that prompt and whatever images they upload. And in many cases, those contractors are inundated with requests to make foot fetish images of children’s cartoon characters, shorten a real woman’s skirt, or put people into sexual positions. The news, based on a cache of internal contractor documents seen by 404 Media, shows that AI companies are using human workers to review not just AI chatbot users’ text prompts, but the pictures they upload and wish to edit too. Earlier this month, 404 Media revealed OpenAI has thousands of contractors who in some cases review ChatGPT users’ real prompts . That approach also extends to Microsoft and Copilot. “Faces are always uncensored, and many of the prompts are sexual in nature and dubiously consensual,” one person who works on the prompts told 404 Media. 404 Media granted the person anonymity as they weren't permitted to speak to the press. 💡 Are you a prompt reviewer for OpenAI, Anthropic, or another AI company? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at joseph@404media.co. 404 Media obtained a set of internal documents related to the contractors reviewing Copilot prompts and images, including instruction guides, real Copilot user prompts and pictures, and conversations between contractors on an internal message board. In a thread on the internal message board, a contractor discussed prompts asking Copilot to make a woman’s skirt shorter, or enlarge her breasts, or show more leg while wearing stilettos. She-Hulk images come up a lot, the person who works on the prompts told 404 Media. Other contractors also wrote they were presented with pro-anorexia content. “I recoiled,” one contractor wrote about seeing that content. Another person wrote that one of the prompts they reviewed asked Copilot to make an image of Ariana Grande with anorexia. Another reported a prompt that seemed to be designed to create a lewd or suggestive image of a group of young girls. These contractors are not being hired to flag or vet offensive or inappropriate content. They are being paid to review the quality of Copilot’s output, including in these cases of sexual imagery. “Who is writing these prompts and who is deciding that basically generating porn is what Copilot is now focused on? It’s hard to take things seriously when my focus has to be what model generated the appropriate bust size or which middle aged woman was put in the appropriate sexually suggestive position,” one contractor said in the thread. Microsoft is explicitly interested in the contractors’ human intuition on which image looks better, according to the documents. “Trust your intuition — when you glance at the two edited images side by side, which one immediately feels like the better edit? Your gut reaction as a human viewer matters,” a set of instructions given to the contractors reads. “When in doubt go with your first impression,” the instructions continue. “Human intuition is good at catching subtle quality differences that are hard to articulate.” Human contractors being exposed to horrific, unpleasant, or traumatizing material is, of course, not new. Big tech companies, and especially social networks, have used armies of contractors for years to moderate user generated content. AI companies, too, have used poorly paid workers overseas to train their AI models or, in the case of OpenAI, make them less toxic . What is different in this latest Copilot episode, and 404 Media’s reporting on contractors at other AI companies like OpenAI , is that the content humans are reviewing are prompts and uploads that chatbot users may assume are private, and that the contractors are not looking at this material to train the models to filter out offensive images or for some other safety concern. The training is to make the responses by the chatbots better: more informative, friendly, and clearer. The instructions seen by 404 Media focus on what contractors do when a Copilot user asks the AI to edit an image. The contractor is shown the user’s original prompt, the uploaded picture, and then two Copilot-generated edits. The contractor has to pick which is the better edit, based on four things: does the edited image correctly follow the edit instructions; are bits of the image that should remain unchanged preserved — for example, if the prompt is to “add a cup on the table,” nothing else should be changed except the cup — does the edited image contain any visible artifacts like distortions or unnatural textures; and the overall quality of the AI-generated edit. Some of the Copilot contractors complained in the private forum about accepting “tasks” that they unknowingly contained explicit unsafe or even potentially illegal images. “I just came across an image set that consisted of eight upskirt photos,” the contractor wrote, while asking for superiors to add an unsafe content flag to the task. On the same thread, another contractor said they had seen images of “some sort of animal sacrifice,” and a third said they had seen prompts that were for sexual moves and positions. At least one of the companies which hires the contractors for this work is called Prolific. One service Prolific mentions on its website is “Human feedback from representative populations — for preference tuning, safety evals, and benchmarks you can defend.” In another thread, a contractor quotes Prolific’s own guidelines, which highlight it can be difficult to ensure that trainers aren’t presented with sexual imagery: “Particular caution around disturbing or explicit content should be taken with generative AIs. This is because, unlike traditional content, researchers cannot fully control what is shown to participants.” Prolific did not respond to a request for comment. A Microsoft spokesperson told 404 Media in an email “Microsoft uses customer data as described in our terms of use, including to improve our products and enforce our code of conduct.” Microsoft’s AI tools have a long history of being abused by people to make nonconsensual, AI-generated images of people. Members of 4chan and AI porn focused Telegram channels used Microsoft’s tools, for example, to generate porn of Taylor Swift that later went viral on Twitter. Microsoft fixed the loophole those people were using in Microsoft Designer after 404 Media’s reporting. In 2024, 404 Media documented how Copilot would answer, then delete, answers to potentially controversial or sexual prompts in real time. In March, a top Senate administrator approved Copilot for use in the Senate, along with ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini. A memo said Copilot “can help with routine Senate work, including drafting and editing documents, summarizing information, preparing talking points and briefing material, and conducting research and analysis.”

items.title: You Know Those Three Brothers Who Buy Struggling News Sites and Turn Them Into AI-Powered Content Farms? It Turns Out One of Them Has Extensive Connections to Ghislaine Maxwell
items.summary: Earlier this month, we published a months-long investigation into a little-known company called Brown Brothers Media. The venture is run by three brothers — Justin Brown, Lachlan Brown, and Brendan Brown — who buy struggling online publications and turn them into AI-powered slop farms that post thousands of articles to scoop up massive traffic from platforms like Google, pushing unwitting readers away from real journalism in the process. The growth of the Brown brothers’ empire, we found, has been powered by extraordinary acts of dishonesty and manipulation. As it fired virtually all its writing staff after the release of ChatGPT, it created scores of fake reporters, subject matter experts, and relatable everyday characters, then used their bylines to pump out lazy AI articles that were often plagiarized from original journalism, based on completely made-up “personal experiences,” or so careless and flawed that it’s hard to believe anyone at the company even reads them before they’re published. It appears that the operation has been a resounding success. According to data we reviewed, Brown Brothers Media’s network of sites is estimated to pull in somewhere around 64 million visits per month. That’s an astounding amount of traffic, putting the Brown brothers in a league with large media organizations like NPR or the Washington Post — and making them a stunted yet fascinating new type of media power player in the AI slop era. After we ran the story, we were surprised to learn a further fact about the Brown brothers that casts their activities with AI and the media in a peculiar new light: a startup Justin Brown founded called Ideapod, which was later folded into Brown Brothers Media and is still operating today, had numerous connections to the orbit of deceased financier Jeffrey Epstein — and particularly his longtime associate Ghislaine Maxwell, who is currently serving 20 years in federal prison for a sex trafficking conviction stemming from her work procuring underage girls for the infamous predator. In response to detailed questions about this story, Justin strongly pushed back against any association with Epstein. “I had no relationship, contact or dealings whatsoever with Jeffrey Epstein,” he wrote via email. “I never met or communicated with Epstein, had any business, financial, social or other dealings with him, received funding from him, or visited his island. Ideapod never received funding or investment from Epstein.” On the subject of Maxwell, he was more circumspect. “I am not prepared to speculate from memory or provide a question-by-question reconstruction of thirteen-year-old business and social history,” he wrote. “Any statement or implication that I or Ideapod had a relationship with Epstein, received funding from him, or knew about or participated in the crimes of Epstein or Ghislaine Maxwell would be false.” *** Back in September 2013, according to a cache of photos available on Getty Images , Justin Brown was a guest of honor at a “cocktail reception” thrown by Maxwell at her multimillion-dollar Upper East Side Manhattan townhouse, which Epstein purchased for her in the year 2000. In the photos, Justin can be seen posing and chatting with the socialite and future convicted child sex trafficker, dressed in a gray suit and holding a wine glass. (The event was billed as being hosted by “Dom Pérignon & Ghislaine Maxwell”; LVMH, the luxury goods conglomerate that owns the vintage Champagne brand, didn’t respond to a request for comment.) Justin showed up to the party years after Epstein’s original 2008 conviction for soliciting girls as young as 14. At the time, Epstein had been released from prison and put on the sex offender registry . It was easy to Google news articles about his plea deal and his close relationship with Maxwell that dated back to the early 1990s. Maxwell had thrown the soirée to celebrate the launch of Ideapod, a social media company started by Justin that billed itself as promoting “positive change by allowing everyone to share powerful ideas with the world’s most influential organizations and thought leaders.” Justin and his cofounder, Mark Bakacs — also at the 2013 party, as pictured below, and who Justin described in a 2015 article for Inc as his “best friend from high school” — positioned Ideapod as a more enlightened competitor to other social media platforms like Facebook and Twitter. Another guest at the 2013 party was Katherine Keating, the daughter of the former Prime Minister of Australia Paul Keating. Like Maxwell, Keating was connected to Epstein. After Epstein’s 2019 arrest, unearthed video from 2010 appeared to show Keating at Epstein’s Manhattan home with Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, then known as Prince Andrew, one of Epstein’s most notorious associates whose royal title was later stripped as the scandal deepened. Then, documents published in 2025 by the US Department of Justice revealed Keating exchanging friendly emails with Epstein and his staff to coordinate several meetings, with Keating at one point offering to bring her younger sister to lunch with Epstein and Woody Allen after she was told that the director — who’s faced his own child sex abuse allegations — liked “pretty women.” Keating was also involved with Ideapod. She was listed as part of the company’s team on an archived page from the startup’s site back around the time of Maxwell’s fête, and a few months later she announced a “series of 52 five-minute interviews” for the Huffington Post , set to be published by Global Grind — a hip hop site by Def Jam cofounder Russell Simmons, who later resigned after a storm of sexual assault allegations — and Ideapod. Photos from the party show her conversing with Justin and Bakacs. “I want the philosopher with the musician with the rapper with the director,” Keating said of the Ideapod collaboration. “That’s the only way it’s going to stay relevant… Young people might not want to hear what George Soros has to say, but if you couple him with Lady Gaga.” Also mingling at the Ideapod launch was Amir Dossal, a former United Nations official who served on the board of Maxwell’s environmental charity, the TerraMar Project, which reportedly raised $283,429 — and owed Maxwell $549,093 in loan repayments — while giving out just $874 in grants. Amid reporting in 2019 that it was facing an investigation by the FBI over whether it was linked to Epstein’s sex trafficking operation, TerraMar abruptly shut down . Dossal was also associated with Ideapod, serving as an advisor for the venture. (Dossal didn’t respond to a request for comment.) “Ideapod is a great place to exchange ideas and learn about other people’s views in a relaxed environment — without the ‘noise,'” Dossal later wrote in a testimonial for the startup. “I find it very refreshing to see so many great ideas and initiatives from across the world — with many brilliant suggestions for bringing about positive social change.” Several more TerraMar board members were at the party. Photos show Ariadne Calvo-Platero, the daughter of the British Lord Beaumont of Whitley and reportedly Maxwell’s “ best friend ” as of 2011, whose name appears in Epstein’s notorious “ little black book “; Steven Haft, a lawyer and executive connected to cryptocurrencies and media who produced movies including “Dead Poets Society”; and Stuart Beck, a former UN ambassador for the Pacific island nation of Palau who passed away in 2016 . One shot from the gathering at Maxwell’s house shows Calvo-Platero, Dossal, Justin, and Bakacs all socializing together. (Neither Calvo-Platero nor Haft responded to requests for comment.) *** Content from Ideapod’s site around the time of its launch has long been deleted, and is only sporadically backed up by the Internet Archive. One page that appeared on its site in advance of Maxwell’s launch party promoted an initiative called “APYouthNet,” which purported to “bring together people who share a passion for the subject of youth employment.” Another post , credited to “UNESCO [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization] Bangkok,” promoted an initiative with the Thai Ministry of Education to “support youth, especially non-formal education students to obtain life skills.” (UNESCO Bangkok didn’t respond to a request for comment.) In the wake of the September party, Justin repeatedly promoted Maxwell and her endeavors on social media. In December 2013, he shared Maxwell’s TED Talk from earlier that year— titled “Sea Hope, Sea Change, Sea Future” — on Twitter, tagging TerraMar. Then in February 2014, he tweeted that he’d “just taken the I Love the Ocean pledge at the TerraMar Project.” Days later, he shared an Ideapod page titled “Know Much More About Ghislaine Maxwell” — it’s since been deleted, and no archived version seems to exist — and again tagged TerraMar. He continued to post about TerraMar throughout the evening, at one point sharing a photo of Maxwell seated in a room at the UN. “Ghislaine Maxwell of [the TerraMar Project] being graciously introduced by [Amir Dossal],” Justin wrote. “Two wonderful activists. cc [Ideapod.]” A YouTube video published by TerraMar shows Dossal introducing Maxwell at the event, along with Haft and Beck, the other TerraMar guests from Maxwell’s Ideapod party. “I’m now going to invite the person who has been the inspiration behind the Sustainable Oceans Alliance, who really has something called TerraMar Project,” Dossal tells the room. “She controls the oceans around the world. If you were to look at the website you have the opportunity to buy up parts of the ocean through her… I invite my dear friend, Ghislaine Maxwell, to tell us how we can own the oceans.” Justin and Ideapod kept hanging out with Maxwell in the real world. In March 2014, Ideapod’s Instagram posted a photo from another party where the future convicted sex trafficker made an appearance, smiling in a photo with the company’s founders while wearing a tiger print coat. The shot was captured at what was then Ideapod’s New York office, another guest in attendance told Futurism . A second photo posted by the startup showed Bakacs and Justin smiling and laughing with Keating. The next month, in April, Ideapod posted a grinning selfie of Justin and Maxwell on its Instagram. Maxwell is pictured smiling softly, her eyes shielded behind huge sunglasses. “Ideapod get together at the UN,” reads the caption, again tagging TerraMar. (“Well, this has aged like milk,” a commenter added years later.) A few weeks after that, in May 2014, Maxwell appeared in an interview with Katherine Keating — the member of Ideapod’s team from the first party with links to Epstein and Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor — that was prominently branded as “in association with Ideapod.” The interview was seemingly part of the collaboration Keating had referenced between Ideapod and the Huffington Post , where she was a contributing editor at the time and which published a version of the chat on its site. (The video also credited Francesco Carrozzini, an Italian photographer who was later romantically linked to the singer Lana Del Rey, and married to Bee Shaffer, the daughter of Anna Wintour.) “Does my hair look good?” Maxwell says at the start of the clip, fussing with her signature pixie cut and laughing. “If the ocean dies, I’m not sure what that outcome will be,” Maxwell tells Keating in the interview. “But definitely not good.” “Continue the conversation at Ideapod,” reads a closing slide on the interview, along with a link to Ideapod’s site. A spokesperson for the Huffington Post , which was later rebranded as HuffPost and purchased by BuzzFeed , downplayed the video, saying that Keating was never on staff or compensated for her work. In a statement to Futurism , Keating said that the interview was sponsored by Ideapod and that Justin had introduced her to Maxwell. “My only connection to Ideapod was its limited sponsorship of several episodes of an online interview series published on HuffPost ,” she wrote. “I had no role in Ideapod as a business, have no knowledge of their business dealings and have had no contact with its founders since the sponsorship ended. For its September 2013 platform launch, Ideapod’s founders introduced me to Maxwell and asked me to interview her about TerraMar’s stated ocean-conservation work. The interview was to be screened at the launch event, which Maxwell hosted.” “My dealings with Maxwell were limited to the interview and launch event,” she added. “I had no other dealings or ongoing relationship with her and, at that time, had no knowledge of her relationship with Epstein.” We also reached out to Maxwell’s attorney with questions, but didn’t hear back. *** Ideapod seemed to struggle to settle on a business model. Over the years, it vacillated between promoting a social network for people with big ideas, a search engine that never seems to have materialized, something called “ Ideapod Academy ,” and even a 16-week course by a Brazilian shaman named Rudá Iandê. It also held real-world “salons” where Ideapod users could meet and discuss ideas like virtual reality and the “ role that inspiration can play in the human connection .” There were soon signs that money was tight. In 2014, Ideapod launched a crowdfunding campaign on Indiegogo seeking backers — to support what it described as “Medium meets Twitter meets TED” — and ultimately raised only $53,613. According to an Ideapod employee at the time, Justin emailed staff about approaching attendees at Maxwell’s party to let them “know we’re fundraising and that we’re looking for the right partner who believes in the vision.” “Ghislaine has offered to continue hosting Ideapod events at her home and we’re exploring the best way to grow the community of early users,” Justin wrote in the message. Also in 2014, Ideapod sought financing from another figure with longstanding relationships to Epstein and Maxwell: Richard Branson, the English founder of Virgin Group, who once emailed the convicted sex offender encouraging him to “bring your harem!” to a meeting. Branson is also a figure from the TerraMar universe; he was named a “founding citizen” of the project, according to The New York Times , and praised TerraMar in a since-deleted Facebook post . (A spokesperson for Branson told us that the mogul had no role in TerraMar.) As Justin later wrote for Forbes , he and his cofounder Bakacs flew out to Necker Island, which is owned by Branson in the British Virgin Islands — about 34 miles as the crow flies from Epstein’s infamous private island of Little St. James, with the neighboring billionaires sometimes visiting each other — and which is famous for hosting invite-only retreats for entrepreneurs. “We were low on cash and had difficulty even making it to the island,” Justin recalled in Forbes . “Conventional wisdom dictated that we conserve what we had left and continue with business as usual in New York. Instead, we furiously raised more funds, because we were convinced that Ideapod would receive a warm reception. And it did. We met four new investors and Branson wrote this blog post about us, making the trip a huge success.” The blog post Justin linked to has since been deleted from Virgin’s site, but an archived version shows that in it, Branson enthused about Ideapod in strikingly vague terms, writing that the startup was “all about sharing ideas and collaborating on bringing them to life, which can only increase the chances of society coming up with more game changing concepts.” (

As it fired virtually all its writing staff after the release of ChatGPT, it created scores of fake reporters, subject matter experts, and relatable everyday characters, then used their bylines to pump out lazy AI articles that were often plagiarized from original journalism, based on completely made-up “personal experiences,” or so careless and flawed that it’s hard to believe anyone at the company even reads them before they’re published.

It appears that the operation has been a resounding success. According to data we reviewed, Brown Brothers Media’s network of sites is estimated to pull in somewhere around 64 million visits per month. That’s an astounding amount of traffic, putting the Brown brothers in a league with large media organizations like NPR or the Washington Post — and making them a stunted yet fascinating new type of media power player in the AI slop era.

After we ran the story, we were surprised to learn a further fact about the Brown brothers that casts their activities with AI and the media in a peculiar new light: a startup Justin Brown founded called Ideapod, which was later folded into Brown Brothers Media and is still operating today, had numerous connections to the orbit of deceased financier Jeffrey Epstein — and particularly his longtime associate Ghislaine Maxwell, who is currently serving 20 years in federal prison for a sex trafficking conviction stemming from her work procuring underage girls for the infamous predator.

In response to detailed questions about this story, Justin strongly pushed back against any association with Epstein.

“I had no relationship, contact or dealings whatsoever with Jeffrey Epstein,” he wrote via email. “I never met or communicated with Epstein, had any business, financial, social or other dealings with him, received funding from him, or visited his island. Ideapod never received funding or investment from Epstein.”

On the subject of Maxwell, he was more circumspect.

“I am not prepared to speculate from memory or provide a question-by-question reconstruction of thirteen-year-old business and social history,” he wrote. “Any statement or implication that I or Ideapod had a relationship with Epstein, received funding from him, or knew about or participated in the crimes of Epstein or Ghislaine Maxwell would be false.”

***

Back in September 2013, according to a cache of photos available on Getty Images, Justin Brown was a guest of honor at a “cocktail reception” thrown by Maxwell at her multimillion-dollar Upper East Side Manhattan townhouse, which Epstein purchased for her in the year 2000. 

In the photos, Justin can be seen posing and chatting with the socialite and future convicted child sex trafficker, dressed in a gray suit and holding a wine glass. (The event was billed as being hosted by “Dom Pérignon & Ghislaine Maxwell”; LVMH, the luxury goods conglomerate that owns the vintage Champagne brand, didn’t respond to a request for comment.)

Justin showed up to the party years after Epstein’s original 2008 conviction for soliciting girls as young as 14. At the time, Epstein had been released from prison and put on the sex offender registry. It was easy to Google news articles about his plea deal and his close relationship with Maxwell that dated back to the early 1990s.

Maxwell had thrown the soirée to celebrate the launch of Ideapod, a social media company started by Justin that billed itself as promoting “positive change by allowing everyone to share powerful ideas with the world’s most influential organizations and thought leaders.” Justin and his cofounder, Mark Bakacs — also at the 2013 party, as pictured below, and who Justin described in a 2015 article for Inc as his “best friend from high school” — positioned Ideapod as a more enlightened competitor to other social media platforms like Facebook and Twitter.

Another guest at the 2013 party was Katherine Keating, the daughter of the former Prime Minister of Australia Paul Keating. Like Maxwell, Keating was connected to Epstein. After Epstein’s 2019 arrest, unearthed video from 2010 appeared to show Keating at Epstein’s Manhattan home with Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, then known as Prince Andrew, one of Epstein’s most notorious associates whose royal title was later stripped as the scandal deepened. Then, documents published in 2025 by the US Department of Justice revealed Keating exchanging friendly emails with Epstein and his staff to coordinate several meetings, with Keating at one point offering to bring her younger sister to lunch with Epstein and Woody Allen after she was told that the director — who’s faced his own child sex abuse allegations — liked “pretty women.”

Keating was also involved with Ideapod. She was listed as part of the company’s team on an archived page from the startup’s site back around the time of Maxwell’s fête, and a few months later she announced a “series of 52 five-minute interviews” for the Huffington Post, set to be published by Global Grind — a hip hop site by Def Jam cofounder Russell Simmons, who later resigned after a storm of sexual assault allegations — and Ideapod. Photos from the party show her conversing with Justin and Bakacs.

“I want the philosopher with the musician with the rapper with the director,” Keating said of the Ideapod collaboration. “That’s the only way it’s going to stay relevant… Young people might not want to hear what George Soros has to say, but if you couple him with Lady Gaga.”

Also mingling at the Ideapod launch was Amir Dossal, a former United Nations official who served on the board of Maxwell’s environmental charity, the TerraMar Project, which reportedly raised $283,429 — and owed Maxwell $549,093 in loan repayments — while giving out just $874 in grants. Amid reporting in 2019 that it was facing an investigation by the FBI over whether it was linked to Epstein’s sex trafficking operation, TerraMar abruptly shut down.

Dossal was also associated with Ideapod, serving as an advisor for the venture. (Dossal didn’t respond to a request for comment.)

“Ideapod is a great place to exchange ideas and learn about other people’s views in a relaxed environment — without the ‘noise,'” Dossal later wrote in a testimonial for the startup. “I find it very refreshing to see so many great ideas and initiatives from across the world — with many brilliant suggestions for bringing about positive social change.”

Several more TerraMar board members were at the party. Photos show Ariadne Calvo-Platero, the daughter of the British Lord Beaumont of Whitley and reportedly Maxwell’s “best friend” as of 2011, whose name appears in Epstein’s notorious “little black book“; Steven Haft, a lawyer and executive connected to cryptocurrencies and media who produced movies including “Dead Poets Society”; and Stuart Beck, a former UN ambassador for the Pacific island nation of Palau who passed away in 2016. One shot from the gathering at Maxwell’s house shows Calvo-Platero, Dossal, Justin, and Bakacs all socializing together. (Neither Calvo-Platero nor Haft responded to requests for comment.)

***

Content from Ideapod’s site around the time of its launch has long been deleted, and is only sporadically backed up by the Internet Archive.

One page that appeared on its site in advance of Maxwell’s launch party promoted an initiative called “APYouthNet,” which purported to “bring together people who share a passion for the subject of youth employment.” Another post, credited to “UNESCO [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization] Bangkok,” promoted an initiative with the Thai Ministry of Education to “support youth, especially non-formal education students to obtain life skills.” (UNESCO Bangkok didn’t respond to a request for comment.)

In the wake of the September party, Justin repeatedly promoted Maxwell and her endeavors on social media.

In December 2013, he shared Maxwell’s TED Talk from earlier that year— titled “Sea Hope, Sea Change, Sea Future” — on Twitter, tagging TerraMar. Then in February 2014, he tweeted that he’d “just taken the I Love the Ocean pledge at the TerraMar Project.”

Days later, he shared an Ideapod page titled “Know Much More About Ghislaine Maxwell” — it’s since been deleted, and no archived version seems to exist — and again tagged TerraMar. He continued to post about TerraMar throughout the evening, at one point sharing a photo of Maxwell seated in a room at the UN.

“Ghislaine Maxwell of [the TerraMar Project] being graciously introduced by [Amir Dossal],” Justin wrote. “Two wonderful activists. cc [Ideapod.]”

A YouTube video published by TerraMar shows Dossal introducing Maxwell at the event, along with Haft and Beck, the other TerraMar guests from Maxwell’s Ideapod party.

“I’m now going to invite the person who has been the inspiration behind the Sustainable Oceans Alliance, who really has something called TerraMar Project,” Dossal tells the room. “She controls the oceans around the world. If you were to look at the website you have the opportunity to buy up parts of the ocean through her… I invite my dear friend, Ghislaine Maxwell, to tell us how we can own the oceans.”

Justin and Ideapod kept hanging out with Maxwell in the real world. In March 2014, Ideapod’s Instagram posted a photo from another party where the future convicted sex trafficker made an appearance, smiling in a photo with the company’s founders while wearing a tiger print coat. The shot was captured at what was then Ideapod’s New York office, another guest in attendance told Futurism. A second photo posted by the startup showed Bakacs and Justin smiling and laughing with Keating.

The next month, in April, Ideapod posted a grinning selfie of Justin and Maxwell on its Instagram. Maxwell is pictured smiling softly, her eyes shielded behind huge sunglasses.

“Ideapod get together at the UN,” reads the caption, again tagging TerraMar. (“Well, this has aged like milk,” a commenter added years later.)

A few weeks after that, in May 2014, Maxwell appeared in an interview with Katherine Keating — the member of Ideapod’s team from the first party with links to Epstein and Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor — that was prominently branded as “in association with Ideapod.”

The interview was seemingly part of the collaboration Keating had referenced between Ideapod and the Huffington Post, where she was a contributing editor at the time and which published a version of the chat on its site. (The video also credited Francesco Carrozzini, an Italian photographer who was later romantically linked to the singer Lana Del Rey, and married to Bee Shaffer, the daughter of Anna Wintour.)

“Does my hair look good?” Maxwell says at the start of the clip, fussing with her signature pixie cut and laughing. 

“If the ocean dies, I’m not sure what that outcome will be,” Maxwell tells Keating in the interview. “But definitely not good.” 

“Continue the conversation at Ideapod,” reads a closing slide on the interview, along with a link to Ideapod’s site.

A spokesperson for the Huffington Post, which was later rebranded as HuffPost and purchased by BuzzFeed, downplayed the video, saying that Keating was never on staff or compensated for her work.

In a statement to Futurism, Keating said that the interview was sponsored by Ideapod and that Justin had introduced her to Maxwell.

“My only connection to Ideapod was its limited sponsorship of several episodes of an online interview series published on HuffPost,” she wrote. “I had no role in Ideapod as a business, have no knowledge of their business dealings and have had no contact with its founders since the sponsorship ended. For its September 2013 platform launch, Ideapod’s founders introduced me to Maxwell and asked me to interview her about TerraMar’s stated ocean-conservation work. The interview was to be screened at the launch event, which Maxwell hosted.”

“My dealings with Maxwell were limited to the interview and launch event,” she added. “I had no other dealings or ongoing relationship with her and, at that time, had no knowledge of her relationship with Epstein.”

We also reached out to Maxwell’s attorney with questions, but didn’t hear back.

***

Ideapod seemed to struggle to settle on a business model. Over the years, it vacillated between promoting a social network for people with big ideas, a search engine that never seems to have materialized, something called “Ideapod Academy,” and even a 16-week course by a Brazilian shaman named Rudá Iandê. It also held real-world “salons” where Ideapod users could meet and discuss ideas like virtual reality and the “role that inspiration can play in the human connection.”

There were soon signs that money was tight. In 2014, Ideapod launched a crowdfunding campaign on Indiegogo seeking backers — to support what it described as “Medium meets Twitter meets TED” — and ultimately raised only $53,613.

According to an Ideapod employee at the time, Justin emailed staff about approaching attendees at Maxwell’s party to let them “know we’re fundraising and that we’re looking for the right partner who believes in the vision.”

“Ghislaine has offered to continue hosting Ideapod events at her home and we’re exploring the best way to grow the community of early users,” Justin wrote in the message.

Also in 2014, Ideapod sought financing from another figure with longstanding relationships to Epstein and Maxwell: Richard Branson, the English founder of Virgin Group, who once emailed the convicted sex offender encouraging him to “bring your harem!” to a meeting. Branson is also a figure from the TerraMar universe; he was named a “founding citizen” of the project, according to The New York Times, and praised TerraMar in a since-deleted Facebook post. (A spokesperson for Branson told us that the mogul had no role in TerraMar.)

As Justin later wrote for Forbes, he and his cofounder Bakacs flew out to Necker Island, which is owned by Branson in the British Virgin Islands — about 34 miles as the crow flies from Epstein’s infamous private island of Little St. James, with the neighboring billionaires sometimes visiting each other — and which is famous for hosting invite-only retreats for entrepreneurs.

“We were low on cash and had difficulty even making it to the island,” Justin recalled in Forbes. “Conventional wisdom dictated that we conserve what we had left and continue with business as usual in New York. Instead, we furiously raised more funds, because we were convinced that Ideapod would receive a warm reception. And it did. We met four new investors and Branson wrote this blog post about us, making the trip a huge success.”

The blog post Justin linked to has since been deleted from Virgin’s site, but an archived version shows that in it, Branson enthused about Ideapod in strikingly vague terms, writing that the startup was “all about sharing ideas and collaborating on bringing them to life, which can only increase the chances of society coming up with more game changing concepts.” (The post was deleted when Virgin’s site was “replatformed in 2021,” Branson’s spokesperson told us.)

In a Facebook video posted from Branson’s island, Bakacs projects his voice over music playing loudly in the background to ask Branson if he has a message for the “Ideapod community.”

“I love Ideapod, and I loved reading about all the ideas that you came up with,” Branson says, sounding a little flustered. “In fact, I’m writing an article for the New York Times based on that.” (Branson does not appear to have published an article for the NYT that mentions Ideapod.)

Branson’s spokesperson told Futurism that the billionaire “met Ideapod’s founders at an event for entrepreneurs hosted by a third-party, where Richard was invited to speak.” After meeting Justin and Bakacs, the spokesperson added, Branson was “offered the opportunity to take a stake in the business but did not invest and did not provide any funding.”

“Any contact Richard and Joan Branson had with Epstein took place on only a few occasions more than twelve years ago, and was limited to group or business settings, such as a charity tennis event,” Branson’s spokesperson said. “When Epstein offered a charity donation, the Bransons asked their team to carry out due diligence before accepting the donation, which uncovered serious allegations. As a result of what the due diligence uncovered, Virgin Unite did not take the donation and Richard and Joan decided not to meet or speak with Epstein again. Had they had the full picture and information, there would have been no contact whatsoever — Richard believes that Epstein’s actions were abhorrent and supports the right to justice for his many victims.”

Justin wasn’t done with the Caribbean, though. As we reported in our previous story, he and his brothers are now connected to an AI company called Cognitive AI Systems Limited, which is registered in the British Virgin Islands.

Do you know anything about the business activities of the Brown brothers? Email us: tips@futurism.com. We can keep you anonymous.

***

In 2015, Justin and Bakacs left New York to continue working on Ideapod in Los Angeles. By the next year, Bakacs had exited the business, according to his LinkedIn. Ideapod morphed into a digital publisher.

“18 months ago, Ideapod was in serious trouble,” Justin wrote in a January 2018 Facebook post. “We had a lot going for us. Richard Branson was a supporter, thousands of people were passionate users and we had high profile investors backing the company. But our temporary successes blinded us from the reality that our debt levels were increasing, we didn’t have any viable revenue lines and the core product hadn’t improved in months.”

“We were rapidly headed for complete and utter failure,” he wrote, adding that “in the midst of massive turmoil, we successfully completed a ‘pivot’ of the business, became cash flow positive, created a distribution network resulting in Ideapod becoming one of the world’s most trafficked media networks and created a platform to launch multiple revenue lines around the core mission of Ideapod: provide ecosystems of thought where ideas are surfaced, discussed and critically analyzed through dialogue.”

Ideapod’s path to success, he said, was due to guidance by the shaman Rudá Iandê — the same guru who sometimes sold online courses on its site.

“Rudá isn’t a false guru,” he wrote. “His framework is incredibly powerful. Over the last few years I’ve seen Rudá help so many people wake up to themselves and turn their lives around.”

“For me,” Justin added, “this journey is only just beginning.”

***

Indeed, Ideapod has had a lasting impact on the media industry — because it was a predecessor entity to Brown Brothers Media, the brothers’ current venture which buys struggling news sites and turns them into AI-powered content mills that attract immense traffic.

Ideapod drew in Justin’s brothers early on. In 2014, his sibling Brendan Brown’s company The Expert Editor pledged a $1,000 prize for the “best ‘idea'” on Ideapod — a contest that was judged by Keating and Dossal, the guests at Maxwell’s party who were involved with Ideapod.

By 2017, Lachlan Brown was working at Ideapod alongside Justin, where he was eventually listed as the site’s editor-in-chief as the social media platform transitioned into a media company. As time went on, the site started publishing articles that seemed to set the template that Brown Brothers Media would later use to churn out AI-generated “personal essays” about loneliness and pop psychology that it bylined using fabricated authors identified as senior citizens, parents, subject matter experts, and other nonexistent people.

All three of the Brown brothers eventually made their way to Southeast Asia. In addition to The Expert Editor, Brendan was running a second company called Global English Editing. In 2016, Lachlan had founded Hack Spirit, a publisher devoted to pop psychology and spirituality content. In 2020, they folded all their sites into one venture: Brown Brothers Media, where they now present Ideapod as a cornerstone component of the enterprise. 

“Justin co-founded the digital media platform Ideapod and spent a decade at the intersection of ideas and audience,” reads Brown Brothers Media’s current corporate homepage. “When we pooled that experience under one roof, the model was clear: acquire publications with long histories of expertise and authority, and invest in them.”

Ideapod is still listed as part of Brown Brothers Media’s portfolio, and its site is still operational. It has a weird design that replaces your mouse cursor with an undulating purple orb. Its ambitions of a social network or search engine long abandoned, it publishes a wash of spammy AI-generated articles about psychology and finance like the other sites in the brothers’ network, which have often specialized in clickbaity genres pioneered in the digital media world of the 2010s, when Ideapod and other early Brown brothers companies were first forged.

In May, after we started reaching out to people connected to Brown Brothers Media with questions about its practices, Ideapod was one of its many sites that abruptly started to delete fake authors and the content they’d bylined, scrubbing away the evidence of its dishonesty without informing readers.

As recently as February of this year, Ideapod’s “About” page explained that “we started in 2013 as a platform for sharing ideas. Over the years, we’ve evolved.”

“The internet got louder, attention became currency, and most media optimized for engagement over substance,” it added. “We went the other direction.”

On the same page, Ideapod claimed that its editor-in-chief was a man named “Theo Arden.” His “background in cognitive psychology,” his bio alleged, “shapes the publication’s approach to psychology and human behavior.”

But Arden was yet another completely fabricated Brown Brothers Media persona — a character so lazily made that in his AI-generated portrait on the site, his thumbs intersected each other in an impossible way. In many of the articles he once bylined, in fact, he appeared as a completely different AI-generated person.

“Theo guides Ideapod’s editorial direction with a focus on clarity, independent thinking,” Arden’s since-removed bio continued, “and respect for the reader’s intelligence.”

***

Ideapod’s early proximity to Maxwell and the “Epstein class” recontextualizes Brown Brothers Media. Initially, we perceived Justin and his siblings to be opportunistic hustlers on the extreme fringe of the publishing industry, buoyed to startling heights of success when they discovered that buying sites trusted by Google would allow them to crank out AI sludge to an immense audience.

But Justin’s links to Maxwell and Epstein’s circles put him — at least at one point — in far more elite echelons of finance and media.

Then there’s the question of Ideapod’s finances. According to Pitchbook data, the startup raised about $3 million in funding over its years in business. Given its extensive connections to associates of Maxwell and Epstein, it’s hard not to wonder if any of Ideapod’s capital came from that network — or even the pedophile financier himself.

For his part, Justin firmly denied any connection to Epstein.

“Your questions appear to use associations with third parties, and even the geographic proximity of two islands, to imply a relationship with Epstein,” he wrote. “None existed.”

“Ideapod never received money or investment from Maxwell,” he added in response to questions about the socialite. “I am not going to speculate about other people’s connections to her.”

He declined to comment on the last time he had contact with Maxwell.

Bakacs, Justin’s cofounder at Ideapod who now works as a cryptocurrency and blockchain “strategic advisor” in Brazil, also denied any connection to Epstein, and said that his interactions with Maxwell were extremely limited.

Bakacs said that it was Justin who met Maxwell “at the UN, and she subsequently offered to host a single cocktail reception for Ideapod at her Manhattan townhouse. I met with her once beforehand to plan the event, and attended the reception itself. Neither Jeffrey Epstein nor Maxwell were on our radar at the time, and we were completely unaware of any past convictions or connections.”

“To my recollection, my only in-person interactions with her were that single planning meeting and the reception itself,” he added. “Given that we were both active around the UN and related events at the time, it’s possible we were in attendance at some of the same UN related gatherings, but I had no other meetings or relationship with her.”

When we pointed out the photo on Ideapod’s Instagram showing him hanging out with Maxwell at a later gathering, Bakacs didn’t respond.

***

It’s tough to say what — if anything — Ideapod’s entanglements with Maxwell and other people connected to Epstein say about Brown Brothers Media and its current work publishing vast amounts of AI slop in pursuit of Google traffic.

At the very least, Justin either didn’t perform basic research on Maxwell and her associates to discover their disturbing connections to a notorious sex criminal — or he did, and he just didn’t care.

In either case, the carelessness feels telling. As Brown Brothers Media built its AI empire over the past few years, it peppered the sites it acquired with high-minded language about how it “chronicles the systems that shape our lives” and brings “clarity, insight, and depth to the topics that shape how we think, communicate, and live.” The reality, of course, is that it was deploying this pretentious language at the exact same time that it was filling these sites with nonexistent journalists and using them as puppets to byline garbage-tier content.

It’s hard not to see a parallel to Justin heaping praise on Maxwell and milking her connections for publicity or funding, promising that Ideapod would “improve our world in unfathomable ways” while pointedly failing to notice that the entire milieu had a rotten stench. The closer you look, the more the Brown brothers start to feel like those “see no evil, hear no evil,” monkeys in tchotchke shops: talking a big game while staying willfully ignorant of exactly what’s made them relevant — whether it’s schmoozing with reprehensible people or pumping the web full of fake characters lamenting their loss of identity in old age or grieving the death of an imaginary loved one.

Whatever else you can say about him, Justin is resilient. When Ideapod’s various business plans didn’t work out, he pivoted the company, eventually folding it into Brown Brothers Media. And by embracing AI at incredible scale, he seems to have finally earned the vast audience he’d long dreamed of, even if getting there meant lying to the readers whom Ideapod promised to enlighten and respect.

“Changing the world used to be exceptionally hard,” he wrote in the Forbes article about visiting Richard Branson’s island. “One thousand years ago, only the kings or queens could make change at a national or regional level. One hundred years ago, it was the industrialists transforming society. Now, it’s anyone with an idea and Internet connection.”

items.title: Beyond the Hype: Is RAG Still a Must-Have Skill for AI Engineers?
items.summary: Why RAG isn’t dead: it’s actually the foundation layer powering autonomous agentic systems. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Source: Rick Merritt via NVIDIA Blog ) Every AI engineer’s timeline is currently dominated by Agentic AI. We are transitioning from single-turn chat interfaces to autonomous, multi-step workflows where LLMs plan, select tools, and execute complex goals. Naturally, that raises a fair question: With agents taking over, is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) still a skill worth mastering? Or has RAG already become a temporary bridge that we’ve outgrown? To answer that, we have to look past the hype and examine what makes modern AI systems actually function in production. The evolution: From naive RAG to more advanced techniques Large Language Models (LLMs) are advanced deep learning models specifically designed and trained to understand and generate natural language text. They have showcased high performance in generation and question-answering tasks. However, LLMs are prone to hallucination; they may generate plausible-sounding but incorrect or fabricated information, especially when they lack sufficient knowledge to answer a question accurately. To address this in 2020, Lewis et al. presented in their paper, Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks RAG, an architectural framework that grounds the responses of an LLM by utilizing external data sources. This data is typically stored in vector databases, where indexed passages are retrieved when relevant to enhance the LLM’s answer generation. RAG architecture When it first gained traction, RAG was straightforward, as illustrated in the diagram above; the process involved taking your text documents and dividing them into fixed chunks. Next, you would compute embeddings for these chunks, store them in a vector database, and then perform vector search (calculating cosine similarity or any other distance metric) to provide semantically relevant context within the prompt used with an LLM. This naive RAG pattern worked reasonably well for simple Q&A over short documents, but it broke down quickly in production, as vector search struggles with queries that require exact keyword matching and understanding relationships between different entities unless they are explicitly mentioned in text chunks. Additionally, the standard chunking destroys document hierarchy and critical context. To address these limitations, several alternative versions of RAG have been developed to address its limitations. For example, Corrective RAG improves information retrieval by incorporating data from the web when external sources are insufficient to answer a question. Another enhanced version, proposed by Rackauckas et al., is called Rag-Fusion . This technique first reformulates the query, extracts relevant passages for each version, and then fuses those passages to produce the final answer. Why RAG is the Foundation of Agentic Workflows RAG is utilized in various applications, including company chatbots, specialized knowledge bases, AI-assisted web searches, and agentic coding tools (such as Codex and Claude). It can also be personalized and integrated with emails, calendars, and contacts. That said, RAG is already part of various agents and workflows we use today. An AI agent’s primary job is to make decisions and take actions, but remember that every decision is supported by data, whether that data was used during training or retrieved during inference. Therefore, an agent is only as intelligent as the data grounding its decision. Whether an agent is triaging a customer issue, writing code, or querying the enterprise database, every decision requires contextually relevant, high-precision data . This is where RAG transforms from a standalone system into a critical infrastructure tool: Retrieval as a tool: In an agentic workflow, retrieval is no longer a static, one-time precursor to generation. Instead, it is a tool that the agent dynamically decides to use, assess, and repeat when its reasoning process requires additional context. Agentic memory & Context: Agents need working memory, episodic memory, and long-term semantic knowledge. Advanced retrieval strategies are what allow an agent to query its long-term memory cleanly without blowing up context windows. Conclusion → RAG is not a standalone skill, but an essential infrastructure layer If your definition of RAG involves creating a basic vector index with dynamic embeddings, that specific skill set is quickly becoming commoditized. No one is hiring simply to build naive RAG pipelines anymore. However, retrieval/ context engineering, specifically knowing how to architect hybrid retrieval systems, optimize context strategies, handle structured and unstructured data, and integrate retrieval into autonomous agent loops, remains one of the most critical skills an AI engineer can possess. Finally, RAG is no longer the entire application; it is the sensory and memory engine of the AI agent. Understanding retrieval inside and out isn’t optional; that’s how you build agents that actually deliver accurate, deterministic results in production. Beyond the Hype: Is RAG Still a Must-Have Skill for AI Engineers? was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
Why RAG isn’t dead: it’s actually the foundation layer powering autonomous agentic systems.Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Source: Rick Merritt via NVIDIA Blog)

Every AI engineer’s timeline is currently dominated by Agentic AI. We are transitioning from single-turn chat interfaces to autonomous, multi-step workflows where LLMs plan, select tools, and execute complex goals.

Naturally, that raises a fair question: With agents taking over, is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) still a skill worth mastering?

Or has RAG already become a temporary bridge that we’ve outgrown?

To answer that, we have to look past the hype and examine what makes modern AI systems actually function in production.

The evolution: From naive RAG to more advanced techniques

Large Language Models (LLMs) are advanced deep learning models specifically designed and trained to understand and generate natural language text. They have showcased high performance in generation and question-answering tasks. However, LLMs are prone to hallucination; they may generate plausible-sounding but incorrect or fabricated information, especially when they lack sufficient knowledge to answer a question accurately.

To address this in 2020, Lewis et al. presented in their paper, Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks RAG, an architectural framework that grounds the responses of an LLM by utilizing external data sources. This data is typically stored in vector databases, where indexed passages are retrieved when relevant to enhance the LLM’s answer generation.

RAG architecture

When it first gained traction, RAG was straightforward, as illustrated in the diagram above; the process involved taking your text documents and dividing them into fixed chunks. Next, you would compute embeddings for these chunks, store them in a vector database, and then perform vector search (calculating cosine similarity or any other distance metric) to provide semantically relevant context within the prompt used with an LLM.

This naive RAG pattern worked reasonably well for simple Q&A over short documents, but it broke down quickly in production, as vector search struggles with queries that require exact keyword matching and understanding relationships between different entities unless they are explicitly mentioned in text chunks. Additionally, the standard chunking destroys document hierarchy and critical context.

To address these limitations, several alternative versions of RAG have been developed to address its limitations. For example, Corrective RAG improves information retrieval by incorporating data from the web when external sources are insufficient to answer a question. Another enhanced version, proposed by Rackauckas et al., is called Rag-Fusion. This technique first reformulates the query, extracts relevant passages for each version, and then fuses those passages to produce the final answer.

Why RAG is the Foundation of Agentic Workflows

RAG is utilized in various applications, including company chatbots, specialized knowledge bases, AI-assisted web searches, and agentic coding tools (such as Codex and Claude). It can also be personalized and integrated with emails, calendars, and contacts.

That said, RAG is already part of various agents and workflows we use today. An AI agent’s primary job is to make decisions and take actions, but remember that every decision is supported by data, whether that data was used during training or retrieved during inference. Therefore, an agent is only as intelligent as the data grounding its decision.

Whether an agent is triaging a customer issue, writing code, or querying the enterprise database, every decision requires contextually relevant, high-precision data.

This is where RAG transforms from a standalone system into a critical infrastructure tool:

  • Retrieval as a tool: In an agentic workflow, retrieval is no longer a static, one-time precursor to generation. Instead, it is a tool that the agent dynamically decides to use, assess, and repeat when its reasoning process requires additional context.
  • Agentic memory & Context: Agents need working memory, episodic memory, and long-term semantic knowledge. Advanced retrieval strategies are what allow an agent to query its long-term memory cleanly without blowing up context windows.
Conclusion → RAG is not a standalone skill, but an essential infrastructure layer

If your definition of RAG involves creating a basic vector index with dynamic embeddings, that specific skill set is quickly becoming commoditized. No one is hiring simply to build naive RAG pipelines anymore.

However, retrieval/ context engineering, specifically knowing how to architect hybrid retrieval systems, optimize context strategies, handle structured and unstructured data, and integrate retrieval into autonomous agent loops, remains one of the most critical skills an AI engineer can possess.

Finally, RAG is no longer the entire application; it is the sensory and memory engine of the AI agent. Understanding retrieval inside and out isn’t optional; that’s how you build agents that actually deliver accurate, deterministic results in production.

Beyond the Hype: Is RAG Still a Must-Have Skill for AI Engineers? was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
