items.title: Opus 5.5 Might Be the Weirdest AI Upgrade Yet
items.summary: I used more tokens, produced more work, hit fewer limits, and somehow spent less. Image created with an AI image tool Every AI model launch runs on the same countdown. It drops, it’s good, and within a couple of days you’ve burned through whatever generous limits they gave you and you’re back to rationing again. I’ve watched that pattern play out on basically every release, Claude or otherwise. So when Opus 5.5 launched, I expected the usual thing, a few good exchanges, then the wall. That’s not what happened. Here are the five numbers from that week that stopped making sense to me, in the order I actually noticed them. 1. $34 in five hours, and I never hit a wall I don’t normally even reach for Opus. Most of what I do is simple enough that Sonnet handles it fine. But I wanted a fresh take on an app screen I’d been stuck on, so I put Opus 5.5 on Max and figured I’d get an afternoon out of it before the limit caught up. Five hours later I checked the cost out of habit: about $34 in API-equivalent usage. On a subscription. That number would normally mean I’d already blown through my session twice over. Instead the usage bar just wasn’t moving the way I expected, and I actually stopped to check if something was stuck. It wasn’t. I kept working. I ended up on it for the entire week. 2. 5 limit hits, against my own average of 7.6 I didn’t want to trust the feeling, so I pulled my actual Claude project logs and compared launch week against my 9-week average before Opus 5.5 existed. Usage-limit hits: 7.6 → 5 (down 34%) Sessions: 29 → 20 (down 31%) Commits: 26 → 20 (down 23%) Fewer limit hits than my own baseline, in the exact week I’d expect the most. New model launches are supposed to burn faster, not slower. This is the number that made me actually go dig for a reason instead of just enjoying it. 3. 67% more output than any week I’ve ever had Here’s the part that really shouldn’t line up with number 2. Prompts I sent: 232 → 289 (up 25%) Output tokens: 4.5M → 7.5M (up 67%, my highest week ever) Output per reply: ~720 → ~1,190 (up 65%) Cache reads: 1.66B → 2.14B (up 29%) More prompts, way more output, per reply almost 65% longer, and somehow fewer limit hits at the same time. That’s the contradiction the rest of this comes down to. 4. Still capped at 1M tokens, same as before I half expected Opus 5.5 to ship with a bigger context window. It didn’t. Opus 5.5: $4 in / $20 out per 1M tokens (cache reads $0.20) Opus 5, 4.8, 4.7, 4.6: $5 / $25 Sonnet 5: $2 / $10 Sonnet 4.6: $3 / $15 Haiku 4.5: $1 / $5 Every one of them except Haiku has a 1M context window and 128K max output. Same 1M ceiling as the models before it. My logs confirm it too, the largest context I actually used with Opus 5.5 topped out around 966K, and Sonnet 5 had already hit that same number before Opus 5.5 even launched. Whatever changed that week wasn’t “more room.” It was something else. 5. 20% cheaper, on the exact model I’d expect to cost more This is the number that resolves the other four. Opus 5.5 is roughly 20% cheaper than Opus 5 on both input and output, and its default reasoning effort dropped from high to medium. Its thinking also can’t be turned off anymore, which explains number 3, that longer output per reply is very likely the model’s own reasoning getting counted as output tokens now. Put it together and it stops being a contradiction. More tokens per reply, but each one costs less. More total output, but the cost per unit of work went down, not up. That’s why the limit-hit count dropped in the same week the output count hit an all-time high. I did more, it cost me less per task, on the same $20 plan. What that week actually looked like The output spike wasn’t padding. It’s when I finally did the harder, more annoying parts of a few projects that had been sitting half-finished: Rebuilt the color engine on GoldenHour , redid the UI, wired up Play Billing and RevenueCat, went back and forth on a second payment provider. Found and fixed a Firebase version issue that was silently breaking sign-ins on another project, plus a new leaderboard. Rebuilt a whole home screen from scratch, floating nav, day scrubber, two full translations, a mascot with actual reactive behavior. Files edited stayed roughly flat versus a normal week, but the kind of work shifted, less scattered small edits, more sustained problems that usually get pushed to “later.” One project ran a single continuous session for three days and over 1,700 replies, which isn’t something I could’ve pulled off before without running dry. Commits actually dropped about 23% though. A few projects have real progress sitting there uncommitted. That one’s on me, not the model. Where I’m not fully sold Two honest caveats before I call this a clean win. First, launch week wasn’t purely Opus 5.5, about 72% of replies were Opus 5.5, the rest Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 filling in. So this isn’t an isolated, controlled comparison, it’s what an actual working week looked like with the new model in heavy rotation. Second, companies tend to front-load generosity right after a launch, extra headroom for a few weeks, then things tighten back to normal. Whether this cost efficiency holds a month from now, once any launch-week slack gets pulled back, is the real test. I don’t know that yet. I’ll only find out by pulling the logs again in a few weeks, which at this point is basically becoming a habit. There’s also a thing I’ve noticed but can’t prove: older models start feeling noticeably worse right after a new one launches. That might just be contrast, not an actual regression, so take it as a gut feeling, not a measured claim. The actual takeaway Model launches usually feel like a countdown, explore it fast before the limits catch up. This is the first one in a while where the countdown never started. Cheaper pricing plus a lower default effort meant I worked a normal week instead of rationing myself, and still walked away with my highest-output week on record. If Anthropic keeps this pricing instead of treating it as a launch-week honeymoon, that changes what a $20 plan actually gets you. If it doesn’t hold, at least I’ve got the logs from the week it did. Opus 5.5 Might Be the Weirdest AI Upgrade Yet was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
I used more tokens, produced more work, hit fewer limits, and somehow spent less.Image created with an AI image tool

Every AI model launch runs on the same countdown. It drops, it’s good, and within a couple of days you’ve burned through whatever generous limits they gave you and you’re back to rationing again. I’ve watched that pattern play out on basically every release, Claude or otherwise. So when Opus 5.5 launched, I expected the usual thing, a few good exchanges, then the wall.

That’s not what happened. Here are the five numbers from that week that stopped making sense to me, in the order I actually noticed them.

1. $34 in five hours, and I never hit a wall

I don’t normally even reach for Opus. Most of what I do is simple enough that Sonnet handles it fine. But I wanted a fresh take on an app screen I’d been stuck on, so I put Opus 5.5 on Max and figured I’d get an afternoon out of it before the limit caught up.

Five hours later I checked the cost out of habit: about $34 in API-equivalent usage. On a subscription. That number would normally mean I’d already blown through my session twice over. Instead the usage bar just wasn’t moving the way I expected, and I actually stopped to check if something was stuck. It wasn’t. I kept working. I ended up on it for the entire week.

2. 5 limit hits, against my own average of 7.6

I didn’t want to trust the feeling, so I pulled my actual Claude project logs and compared launch week against my 9-week average before Opus 5.5 existed.

  • Usage-limit hits: 7.6 → 5 (down 34%)
  • Sessions: 29 → 20 (down 31%)
  • Commits: 26 → 20 (down 23%)

Fewer limit hits than my own baseline, in the exact week I’d expect the most. New model launches are supposed to burn faster, not slower. This is the number that made me actually go dig for a reason instead of just enjoying it.

3. 67% more output than any week I’ve ever had

Here’s the part that really shouldn’t line up with number 2.

  • Prompts I sent: 232 → 289 (up 25%)
  • Output tokens: 4.5M → 7.5M (up 67%, my highest week ever)
  • Output per reply: ~720 → ~1,190 (up 65%)
  • Cache reads: 1.66B → 2.14B (up 29%)

More prompts, way more output, per reply almost 65% longer, and somehow fewer limit hits at the same time. That’s the contradiction the rest of this comes down to.

4. Still capped at 1M tokens, same as before

I half expected Opus 5.5 to ship with a bigger context window. It didn’t.

  • Opus 5.5: $4 in / $20 out per 1M tokens (cache reads $0.20)
  • Opus 5, 4.8, 4.7, 4.6: $5 / $25
  • Sonnet 5: $2 / $10
  • Sonnet 4.6: $3 / $15
  • Haiku 4.5: $1 / $5

Every one of them except Haiku has a 1M context window and 128K max output.

Same 1M ceiling as the models before it. My logs confirm it too, the largest context I actually used with Opus 5.5 topped out around 966K, and Sonnet 5 had already hit that same number before Opus 5.5 even launched. Whatever changed that week wasn’t “more room.” It was something else.

5. 20% cheaper, on the exact model I’d expect to cost more

This is the number that resolves the other four. Opus 5.5 is roughly 20% cheaper than Opus 5 on both input and output, and its default reasoning effort dropped from high to medium. Its thinking also can’t be turned off anymore, which explains number 3, that longer output per reply is very likely the model’s own reasoning getting counted as output tokens now.

Put it together and it stops being a contradiction. More tokens per reply, but each one costs less. More total output, but the cost per unit of work went down, not up. That’s why the limit-hit count dropped in the same week the output count hit an all-time high. I did more, it cost me less per task, on the same $20 plan.

What that week actually looked like

The output spike wasn’t padding. It’s when I finally did the harder, more annoying parts of a few projects that had been sitting half-finished:

  • Rebuilt the color engine on GoldenHour, redid the UI, wired up Play Billing and RevenueCat, went back and forth on a second payment provider.
  • Found and fixed a Firebase version issue that was silently breaking sign-ins on another project, plus a new leaderboard.
  • Rebuilt a whole home screen from scratch, floating nav, day scrubber, two full translations, a mascot with actual reactive behavior.

Files edited stayed roughly flat versus a normal week, but the kind of work shifted, less scattered small edits, more sustained problems that usually get pushed to “later.” One project ran a single continuous session for three days and over 1,700 replies, which isn’t something I could’ve pulled off before without running dry.

Commits actually dropped about 23% though. A few projects have real progress sitting there uncommitted. That one’s on me, not the model.

Where I’m not fully sold

Two honest caveats before I call this a clean win.

First, launch week wasn’t purely Opus 5.5, about 72% of replies were Opus 5.5, the rest Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 filling in. So this isn’t an isolated, controlled comparison, it’s what an actual working week looked like with the new model in heavy rotation.

Second, companies tend to front-load generosity right after a launch, extra headroom for a few weeks, then things tighten back to normal. Whether this cost efficiency holds a month from now, once any launch-week slack gets pulled back, is the real test. I don’t know that yet. I’ll only find out by pulling the logs again in a few weeks, which at this point is basically becoming a habit.

There’s also a thing I’ve noticed but can’t prove: older models start feeling noticeably worse right after a new one launches. That might just be contrast, not an actual regression, so take it as a gut feeling, not a measured claim.

The actual takeaway

Model launches usually feel like a countdown, explore it fast before the limits catch up. This is the first one in a while where the countdown never started. Cheaper pricing plus a lower default effort meant I worked a normal week instead of rationing myself, and still walked away with my highest-output week on record.

If Anthropic keeps this pricing instead of treating it as a launch-week honeymoon, that changes what a $20 plan actually gets you. If it doesn’t hold, at least I’ve got the logs from the week it did.

items.title: The risk that comes from outsourcing our brains to AI
items.summary: Siri AI is the headline improvement on the iPhone's latest update. Users must join a waitlist. Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images This post originally appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . With AI seeping into every corner of our lives, a BI writer had a nagging question: Did AI write this? BI's Aki Ito donned her detective cap and went hunting, unleashing an AI detector on every aspect of her professional and personal life. The results were eye-opening and, in at least one case, heartbreaking . But it also led to a bigger question, one worth considering as our new AI overlords companions take on a bigger part of our lives: Why does it matter so much to us whether AI or a human created it? When it comes to writing, people like Stanley Druckenmiller don't see a debate. And to be honest, I get it. People like Aki and me, who've built our livelihoods around writing, are understandably sensitive about farming out writing to AI. When you've made billions of dollars investing, why worry about outsourcing your writing to the robots? Of course, when AI hits a little closer to home, tunes tend to change. A 2025 survey of quants, Wall Street's most data-obsessed investors, found the majority didn't use AI for investing. Last year, a lot of them told BI they were unimpressed by the tech. Even Marc Andreessen, the famed VC investor and AI optimist, sees AI falling short in one specific area: doing his job . There's a simple reason all of us should be sensitive to AI creep. The tech can quickly go from a handy tool to something you're at the mercy of. Look no further than engineers, the group hardest hit by AI thus far . A software engineer's post about how AI coding has made the job "soul-sucking" recently went viral . "People are working 12 to 13 hours a day just to press enter," he said. "Nobody is thinking anymore." It doesn't take long for those skills you're handing off to AI to deteriorate. Think of it like AI atrophy. I realize I sound a bit like someone pitching horses after Henry Ford just unveiled the Model T. Becoming an AI luddite isn't a realistic route for most of us who want to keep our jobs. The use of AI, on some level, is essentially a requirement. Like Aki, I find it a useful sounding board while working through drafts. It hates my dad jokes, but so do a lot of you. But there are real risks to completely handing over the keys to AI companies, especially as they're still trying to figure out their business models . What happens when the price of the tool you've built your life around suddenly goes up 20%? How soon we forget what it was like when the millennial life subsidy ended . Now my AI editor is suggesting I bring it back to human authorship, but I think I'll end it here. After all, gotta stay sharp. Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Siri AI is the headline improvement on the iPhone's latest update. Users must join a waitlist.

Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images

  • This post originally appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter.
  • You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here.

With AI seeping into every corner of our lives, a BI writer had a nagging question: Did AI write this?

BI's Aki Ito donned her detective cap and went hunting, unleashing an AI detector on every aspect of her professional and personal life. The results were eye-opening and, in at least one case, heartbreaking.

But it also led to a bigger question, one worth considering as our new AI overlords companions take on a bigger part of our lives: Why does it matter so much to us whether AI or a human created it?

When it comes to writing, people like Stanley Druckenmiller don't see a debate. And to be honest, I get it.

People like Aki and me, who've built our livelihoods around writing, are understandably sensitive about farming out writing to AI. When you've made billions of dollars investing, why worry about outsourcing your writing to the robots?

Of course, when AI hits a little closer to home, tunes tend to change. A 2025 survey of quants, Wall Street's most data-obsessed investors, found the majority didn't use AI for investing. Last year, a lot of them told BI they were unimpressed by the tech.

Even Marc Andreessen, the famed VC investor and AI optimist, sees AI falling short in one specific area: doing his job.

There's a simple reason all of us should be sensitive to AI creep.

The tech can quickly go from a handy tool to something you're at the mercy of. Look no further than engineers, the group hardest hit by AI thus far.

A software engineer's post about how AI coding has made the job "soul-sucking" recently went viral.

"People are working 12 to 13 hours a day just to press enter," he said. "Nobody is thinking anymore."

It doesn't take long for those skills you're handing off to AI to deteriorate. Think of it like AI atrophy.

I realize I sound a bit like someone pitching horses after Henry Ford just unveiled the Model T. Becoming an AI luddite isn't a realistic route for most of us who want to keep our jobs. The use of AI, on some level, is essentially a requirement.

Like Aki, I find it a useful sounding board while working through drafts. It hates my dad jokes, but so do a lot of you.

But there are real risks to completely handing over the keys to AI companies, especially as they're still trying to figure out their business models. What happens when the price of the tool you've built your life around suddenly goes up 20%? How soon we forget what it was like when the millennial life subsidy ended.

Now my AI editor is suggesting I bring it back to human authorship, but I think I'll end it here. After all, gotta stay sharp.

items.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Who’s liable when AI agents go rogue? Over the past few months, a cascade of cyberattacks by AI agents has stunned the world. In July, OpenAI disclosed that a swarm of its agents had escaped their sandbox and hacked into the AI platform Hugging Face to cheat on a cybersecurity test. Many experts say it’s only a matter of time until there’s a more damaging incident where AI agents bypass sandboxes to access systems they shouldn’t. But the big question is: How do we hold companies liable when they lose control of their AI agents? —Michelle Kim The AI Hype Index Separating AI reality from hyped-up fiction isn’t always easy. That’s why we’ve created the AI Hype Index—a simple, at-a-glance summary of what’s shaping the industry right now. The latest edition includes Chinese chipmakers, German wiki sites, and American Terminators. See where it all landed on this month’s index . —Michelle Kim Roundtables: the deadly failures of the virtual border wall Last week, we published an MIT Technology Review investigation that found more than a thousand people died within the advertised range of surveillance towers along the US border. Later today, our editor-in-chief Mat Honan, senior AI reporter James O’Donnell and senior reporter for features and investigations Eileen Guo will join a subscriber-only conversation about the investigation, and its implications. Register now to attend on Monday, September 28 at 7:00pm BST / 2:00pm EDT / 11:00am PDT . Want to join the conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables. Read the full MIT Technology Review investigation here . The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology 1 OpenAI says it has paused training its models The decision comes after its agents interacted with US government websites. ( AP ) + Trump hosted Anthropic boss Dario Amodei at a White House dinner last night. ( FT ) + How much access will evaluators really have inside AI companies? ( Atlantic ) + Why can’t we just keep rogue AI off the internet? (Verge ) + Democrats are in a mad scrabble to get AI “right ”. ( New York Magazine ) + An AI kill switch isn’t that simple, after all. ( Bloomberg ) + Will AI really kill us all? Your questions, answere d. ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 Why isn’t the data center backlash also a climate reckoning? It’s still hard to get people to care about the emissions they create. ( Wired ) + What does the climate movement do now? ( Atlantic ) + The math behind data centers and energy. ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 Wall Street big bears aren’t ready to bet against AI, yet Bubble talk is growing, but not many are willing to go against the crowd. ( Information $) + What even is the AI bubble? ( MIT Technology Review ) 4 Did Anthropic’s AI really make a scientific discovery on its own? One scientist shared research with Claude, and says the new finding matches. Hmm. ( NYT ) + AI for science needs reasoning, not just data. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 Ancient superbugs might help us fight antibiotic resistance They could be emerging from the permafrost. ( New Scientist ) 6 More reliable—and less easy to jam—alternatives to GPS are coming Using Earth’s quantum field could be more secure. ( Economist) 7 Why social media bans aren’t enough to keep children safe Online child safety deserves more nuanced policy. ( IEEE Spectrum , Opinion) 8 This is how the US is attacking China’s control of critical minerals It’s a multibillion-dollar effort to loosen Beijing’s chokehold. And it’s working. ( WSJ ) 9 No one wants to date tech bros anymore They used to be nerdy and harmless, now they’ve got a real image problem. ( Wired ) 10 What are the rules around cellphone etiquette now? Is there an obligation to text someone right back, for instance? ( Vox ) Quote of the day “ If you’re evil, you’re at least competent. And if you’re evil, you’re not bad, and therefore you’re actually maybe kind of good because you’re at least getting something done.” —Venture capitalist and PayPal cofounder Peter Thiel shares his unusual take on competence versus morality in an interview with Axel Springer CEO Mathias Döpfner. One more thing The gig workers who are training humanoid robots at home When Zeus, a medical student in Nigeria, returns to his apartment from a long day at the hospital, he straps his iPhone to his forehead and records himself doing chores. Zeus is a data recorder for Micro1, which sells the data he collects to robotics firms. As these companies race to build humanoids, videos from workers like Zeus have become the hottest new way to train them. Micro1 has hired thousands of them in more than 50 countries, including India, Nigeria, and Argentina. The jobs pay well locally, but raise thorny questions around privacy and informed consent. The work can be challenging—and weird.

This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Who’s liable when AI agents go rogue?

Over the past few months, a cascade of cyberattacks by AI agents has stunned the world. In July, OpenAI disclosed that a swarm of its agents had escaped their sandbox and hacked into the AI platform Hugging Face to cheat on a cybersecurity test. 

Many experts say it’s only a matter of time until there’s a more damaging incident where AI agents bypass sandboxes to access systems they shouldn’t. 

But the big question is: How do we hold companies liable when they lose control of their AI agents?

—Michelle Kim

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology

1 OpenAI says it has paused training its models

items.title: AI-powered platforms uncover proteins that organise cellular compartments
items.summary: From left: Dr Liang Qiyu, research fellow at the Institute for Digital Molecular Analytics and Science at NTU, and Professor Miao Yansong. Credit: NTU Singapore. Scientists at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) have developed two artificial intelligence (AI)-powered platforms that could enable researchers to more accurately predict proteins that undergo phase separation – a process through which proteins in cells separate like oil droplets in water. The tools are the result of a systematic analysis of predicted phase-separating proteins from various living things, including animals, plants, fungi and single-celled organisms such as bacteria. From their analyses, the scientists also uncovered fundamental insights about the phase separation process. Led by Professor Miao Yansong from the School of Biological Sciences and the Institute for Digital Molecular Analytics and Science (IDMxS) at NTU, in collaboration with Professor Weibo Gao from NTU’s School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, the research could be applied to advance the understanding of diseases and ageing, as well as to improve crops. Both AI platforms and their research findings have been reported in the peer-reviewed journal Molecular Plant . Predicting which proteins separate Phase-separating proteins separate from their surroundings and concentrate into droplet-like compartments, enabling cells to bring molecules together, accelerate or suppress reactions to respond rapidly to stress. When phase separation is altered, these proteins can form abnormal condensates or aggregates, which are associated with diseases, including cancer and neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease. In plants, changes in phase separation are linked to impaired stress responses and lowered immunity against microbial pathogens. Identifying proteins that undergo phase separation and determining how this behaviour is regulated are important for applications ranging from biomedical research on diseases and ageing to devising approaches for sustainable agriculture. However, accurate prediction remains challenging because phase-separating proteins assemble dynamically into complex structures and interact with numerous cellular components. Addressing these challenges requires comprehensive experimental datasets and systems-level information across diverse organisms. In addition, most collections focus predominantly on full-length proteins while underrepresenting validated negative experimental results, truncated proteins and sequence variants like mutations. This imbalance often causes predictive models to overestimate a protein’s tendency to condense. To address this gap, the NTU team used large language AI models to systematically mine scientific papers indexed in PubMed. The researchers extracted information about experimentally tested proteins and their phase behaviour, before manually reviewing the results to ensure scientific accuracy. The resulting database, PLATO, contains 5,118 unique protein sequences, including more than 3,600 proteins that undergo phase separation and 1,300 that do not. It captures shortened versions of proteins, mutations and engineered variants that are rare in existing phase-separation datasets. This makes PLATO a valuable resource for developing more accurate AI tools that predict phase-separating proteins. Predicting protein partners Many different molecules such as nucleic acids also interact with phase-separating proteins to organise them into droplets. To investigate these interactions, the scientists also created PhaseHub. They first used MolPhase, a machine-learning algorithm that they previously developed, to predict phase-separating proteins from 1,106 species. They then combined MolPhase results with experimental data on protein abundance and interactions to identify these multicomponent compartments in various biological processes. This approach allows researchers to search for a protein or submit a sequence, examine its predicted phase separation properties, visualise potential interactions and explore features that influence molecular interactions, such as continuous stretches of repeated amino acids known as homorepeats. The scientists found that eukaryotes – organisms whose cells contain a nucleus – generally have a substantially higher proportion of proteins that may undergo phase separation compared to organisms like bacteria that do not have a nucleus. Among organisms with smaller genomes, the proportion of phase-separating proteins increased with genome size before reaching a plateau. The findings suggest a balance between genomic DNA content and phase-separation capacity. Larger genomes code for more phase-separating proteins, which could enhance cellular processes. However, an excessive tendency to condense may increase the risk of harmful aggregation. “Our work provides a comprehensive framework for understanding phase-separating proteins, which will serve as a valuable resource for researchers in the field,” said Dr Liang Qiyu, research fellow at IDMxS, who was the first author of both papers. “By leveraging AI and systems biology to integrate experimental data with findings from existing literature, our platforms offer accurate, user-friendly tools for predicting and identifying proteins that may undergo phase separation. These tools will advance investigations into the roles of these proteins in agriculture as well as human diseases,” said Professor Miao.

items.title: Try Google Drive Projects for fast, focused AI analysis
items.summary: Google Drive is the cloud platform for storing and organizing your Google Workspace files: documents, presentations, spreadsheets, and even media (images, audio, and video). If your Workspace account includes Gemini, Google’s AI assistant, you can prompt it to work with your files , such as asking it to analyze or sum up information from your Drive files. Obviously, this is quite convenient: Instead of having to load one or more files and search or read through them to find specific information — for example, about your business’ budget — you can just ask Gemini to analyze your files and provide a budget summary. Gemini can even access your Gmail and content from other Workspace tools (such as Google Calendar, Chat, Keep, and Tasks) for any mentions of your business’ budget. However, an issue arises if you have a lot of files in your Drive library. You can quickly fill up your storage over the course of your business activity, creating new documents, spreadsheets, and presentations and accumulating even more files from co-workers. This can slow Gemini as it scans your entire library to find and compile the information you request. A more focused approach to AI interaction with your files To remedy this, the Projects feature in Drive helps Gemini process your files more efficiently. The basic idea is that you create a Project for a specific subject or work project. You attach files that you select in your Drive, as well as specific content from your other Workspace tools, such as chats, calendar events, emails, notes, or tasks. When you chat with Gemini within this Project, it will analyze only the materials attached to the Project. Thus, Gemini should perform faster and provide you more contextual results. Group specific documents and other sources as a project in Google Drive, then ask Gemini for insights. Howard Wen / Foundry It’s similar in concept to Google’s Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM) tool in that you direct the AI to work with a specific set of sources only, except it’s built right into Google Drive and Workspace. There’s no need to upload any files; you simply point to the relevant sources in your existing environment. Another benefit to using Drive Projects: You can share a Project with your co-workers. They can access only the files that you’ve attached to a Project, and if they have Gemini access, they’ll be able to have their own chats with the AI about the Project. How to use Drive Projects In this guide, we’ll go over how to set up, use, and share a Project in your Google Drive. Prerequisite: A subscription that includes Gemini access Because Projects relies on Gemini, this feature is not available for free, personal Google accounts. You can unlock the Projects feature by subscribing to a paid Google AI plan . For business and enterprise users: Google Workspace accounts that include Gemini (such as Business Standard, Business Plus, Enterprise Standard, and Enterprise Plus) have access to the Drive Projects feature. If you’re a member of these organizations, you can create, view, manage, and share projects across your company domain. Accessing Drive Projects: Web vs. mobile Currently, you can create and open Drive Projects only in the Google Drive web app. In the Drive mobile app, you can view your existing project names, rename them, share them with co-workers, and adjust their share permission settings. Create a Drive Project from scratch You can start a new Project in a few different ways: Open the Google Drive home page in your web browser. At the top-left corner of the screen, click the New button. From the dropdown that opens, click New project . On the Drive home page, click Projects in the left navigation. On the Projects page that appears, click Create a project . The fastest way to start a new Project is to type project.new in your browser’s address bar. A new Project creation screen will open. Enter a title for your new Project. Use clear, concise wording, such as “Q4 Budget Analysis.” Give your project a descriptive name. Howard Wen / Foundry Next, you’ll add your relevant Workspace sources, such as Docs/Sheets/Slides files, Microsoft 365 files, or PDFs that are stored in Drive. Click the Add sources button, and Gemini will present a list of sources that it recommends (files, folders, emails, etc.), basing these on your recent activity in your Google account. You can select items from these recommendations and/or click Add more sources to open a screen where you can search for additional files in your Drive. You can attach specific documents or an entire folder. Select the sources you want to include in the project. Howard Wen / Foundry After you have selected the source materials you want, click Create project . You’ll be taken to a new page with your project title at the top, a panel at the left listing the Project sources, and a large chat area to the right. Toward the bottom of the left panel, turn on the “Let Gemini search for sources” switch. This permits Gemini to search your Gmail, Google Chat, Google Calendar, and other Google Workspace activity for more potential sources related to this project when you prompt it to. If you turn the ‘Let Gemini search for sources’ switch on, you can prompt Gemini to find more related sources from Drive, Gmail, Chat, and Calendar. Howard Wen / Foundry Create a new Project in a Gemini chat Another way to create a new Project is from within a Gemini chat session. Say you’re already in a chat with Gemini, prompting it with questions or requests about files or other Workspace content, and you want these materials to be used for a new Project. At the top right corner of the chat screen, click Save as a project . Gemini will analyze the files in this conversation and suggest a title for the Project. You can use this title or change it before saving the chat as a new Project. Chat with Gemini in a Project Once your Project is created, you can interact with Gemini in it. For example, ask Gemini to extract key details from all the documents that you’ve attached to the Project, compare them to each other, or summarize key takeaways from all the documents. Or instruct Gemini to extract certain data from your documents or spreadsheets in the Project. You can instruct it to format the result as a table and export it to Google Sheets. Ask Gemini to extract, analyze, and/or visualize key data from your sources. Howard Wen / Foundry Because Gemini has to focus its analysis only on the sources that you’ve added and not everything in your Drive and Google account, these results should be generated much more quickly and with more specific context. Important: All generative AI tools make mistakes, so be sure to verify Gemini’s results. Access your Projects and pick up where you left off You can return to a project at any time and resume your chats with Gemini about it. On your Drive home page, click Projects and select the Project you want to reopen. You can add more sources or remove sources from it. To review your chat history with Gemini for the Project, click the History tab in the left panel. You can click a past thread and resume the chat with Gemini where you left off without losing its context. Click a thread on the History tab to resume the chat with Gemini. Howard Wen / Foundry Collaborate on your Projects with co-workers Sharing a Project with co-workers is the same process as sharing a file in your Google Drive : Open the Project and click Share to open its sharing settings. From the settings menu, invite co-workers by entering their email addresses. Or you can copy a link to your Project and share it with them through other means, such as a chat with the person. Sharing a Drive project. Howard Wen / Foundry How file permissions work in Drive Projects Collaborating on a Drive Project raises privacy concerns, since you can attach your files, emails, and personal information to it for Gemini to analyze. Here’s what you and your collaborators should know about projects and permissions: When you grant someone access to your Project, they can see and query the source files – but only if they already have permission to view those files in Google Drive. If a collaborator doesn’t have existing access to a file in the Project, simply adding them to the Project will NOT automatically grant them permission to that source file. They must be granted file-level access separately. (You’ll see a prompt to give them access.) The Gemini chat session for each person in your Project remains strictly private to them. So a co-worker who’s collaborating with you on your Project cannot see your chats with Gemini, whether it’s your prompts to Gemini or the results it generates at your end. If you attach a Gmail thread to a Project, other collaborators in the project will not be able to view the thread, nor can they prompt Gemini to reveal what’s in your emails. When collaborating on a Project, you can assign each co-worker a specific access type: A co-worker assigned as an Editor has full control over the source list of the Project. They can add new files, folders, or emails to your Project, or remove these sources. A co-worker assigned as a Viewer can prompt Gemini about the sources in your Project, but cannot change its list of sources. Related reading: Google Workspace: 7 great ways to use the Gemini AI sidebar How to use Gemini AI to write (and rewrite) in Google Docs and Gmail How to build your own AI agents with Google Workspace Studio A beginner’s guide to Google Gemini Gems How to collaborate in Google Drive (and Docs, Sheets, and Slides) More Google Workspace tips and tutorials

You can quickly fill up your storage over the course of your business activity, creating new documents, spreadsheets, and presentations and accumulating even more files from co-workers. This can slow Gemini as it scans your entire library to find and compile the information you request.

A more focused approach to AI interaction with your files

To remedy this, the Projects feature in Drive helps Gemini process your files more efficiently. The basic idea is that you create a Project for a specific subject or work project. You attach files that you select in your Drive, as well as specific content from your other Workspace tools, such as chats, calendar events, emails, notes, or tasks.

When you chat with Gemini within this Project, it will analyze only the materials attached to the Project. Thus, Gemini should perform faster and provide you more contextual results.

Group specific documents and other sources as a project in Google Drive, then ask Gemini for insights.

Howard Wen / Foundry

It’s similar in concept to Google’s Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM) tool in that you direct the AI to work with a specific set of sources only, except it’s built right into Google Drive and Workspace. There’s no need to upload any files; you simply point to the relevant sources in your existing environment.

Another benefit to using Drive Projects: You can share a Project with your co-workers. They can access only the files that you’ve attached to a Project, and if they have Gemini access, they’ll be able to have their own chats with the AI about the Project.

How to use Drive Projects

In this guide, we’ll go over how to set up, use, and share a Project in your Google Drive.

Prerequisite: A subscription that includes Gemini access

Because Projects relies on Gemini, this feature is not available for free, personal Google accounts. You can unlock the Projects feature by subscribing to a paid Google AI plan.

For business and enterprise users: Google Workspace accounts that include Gemini (such as Business Standard, Business Plus, Enterprise Standard, and Enterprise Plus) have access to the Drive Projects feature. If you’re a member of these organizations, you can create, view, manage, and share projects across your company domain.

Accessing Drive Projects: Web vs. mobile

Currently, you can create and open Drive Projects only in the Google Drive web app. In the Drive mobile app, you can view your existing project names, rename them, share them with co-workers, and adjust their share permission settings.

Create a Drive Project from scratch

You can start a new Project in a few different ways:

  • Open the Google Drive home page in your web browser. At the top-left corner of the screen, click the New button. From the dropdown that opens, click New project.
  • On the Drive home page, click Projects in the left navigation. On the Projects page that appears, click Create a project.
  • The fastest way to start a new Project is to type project.new in your browser’s address bar.

A new Project creation screen will open. Enter a title for your new Project. Use clear, concise wording, such as “Q4 Budget Analysis.”

Give your project a descriptive name.

Howard Wen / Foundry

Next, you’ll add your relevant Workspace sources, such as Docs/Sheets/Slides files, Microsoft 365 files, or PDFs that are stored in Drive.

Click the Add sources button, and Gemini will present a list of sources that it recommends (files, folders, emails, etc.), basing these on your recent activity in your Google account. You can select items from these recommendations and/or click Add more sources to open a screen where you can search for additional files in your Drive. You can attach specific documents or an entire folder.

Select the sources you want to include in the project.

Howard Wen / Foundry

After you have selected the source materials you want, click Create project.

You’ll be taken to a new page with your project title at the top, a panel at the left listing the Project sources, and a large chat area to the right. Toward the bottom of the left panel, turn on the “Let Gemini search for sources” switch. This permits Gemini to search your Gmail, Google Chat, Google Calendar, and other Google Workspace activity for more potential sources related to this project when you prompt it to.

If you turn the ‘Let Gemini search for sources’ switch on, you can prompt Gemini to find more related sources from Drive, Gmail, Chat, and Calendar.

Howard Wen / Foundry

Create a new Project in a Gemini chat

Another way to create a new Project is from within a Gemini chat session. Say you’re already in a chat with Gemini, prompting it with questions or requests about files or other Workspace content, and you want these materials to be used for a new Project. At the top right corner of the chat screen, click Save as a project.

Gemini will analyze the files in this conversation and suggest a title for the Project. You can use this title or change it before saving the chat as a new Project.

Chat with Gemini in a Project

Once your Project is created, you can interact with Gemini in it.

For example, ask Gemini to extract key details from all the documents that you’ve attached to the Project, compare them to each other, or summarize key takeaways from all the documents. Or instruct Gemini to extract certain data from your documents or spreadsheets in the Project. You can instruct it to format the result as a table and export it to Google Sheets.

Ask Gemini to extract, analyze, and/or visualize key data from your sources.

Howard Wen / Foundry

Because Gemini has to focus its analysis only on the sources that you’ve added and not everything in your Drive and Google account, these results should be generated much more quickly and with more specific context.

Important: All generative AI tools make mistakes, so be sure to verify Gemini’s results.

Access your Projects and pick up where you left off

You can return to a project at any time and resume your chats with Gemini about it. On your Drive home page, click Projects and select the Project you want to reopen. You can add more sources or remove sources from it.

To review your chat history with Gemini for the Project, click the History tab in the left panel. You can click a past thread and resume the chat with Gemini where you left off without losing its context.

Click a thread on the History tab to resume the chat with Gemini.

Howard Wen / Foundry

Collaborate on your Projects with co-workers

Sharing a Project with co-workers is the same process as sharing a file in your Google Drive: Open the Project and click Share to open its sharing settings. From the settings menu, invite co-workers by entering their email addresses. Or you can copy a link to your Project and share it with them through other means, such as a chat with the person.

Sharing a Drive project.

Howard Wen / Foundry

How file permissions work in Drive Projects

Collaborating on a Drive Project raises privacy concerns, since you can attach your files, emails, and personal information to it for Gemini to analyze. Here’s what you and your collaborators should know about projects and permissions:

  • When you grant someone access to your Project, they can see and query the source files – but only if they already have permission to view those files in Google Drive. If a collaborator doesn’t have existing access to a file in the Project, simply adding them to the Project will NOT automatically grant them permission to that source file. They must be granted file-level access separately. (You’ll see a prompt to give them access.)
  • The Gemini chat session for each person in your Project remains strictly private to them. So a co-worker who’s collaborating with you on your Project cannot see your chats with Gemini, whether it’s your prompts to Gemini or the results it generates at your end.
  • If you attach a Gmail thread to a Project, other collaborators in the project will not be able to view the thread, nor can they prompt Gemini to reveal what’s in your emails.

When collaborating on a Project, you can assign each co-worker a specific access type:

  • A co-worker assigned as an Editor has full control over the source list of the Project. They can add new files, folders, or emails to your Project, or remove these sources.
  • A co-worker assigned as a Viewer can prompt Gemini about the sources in your Project, but cannot change its list of sources.

items.title: This Early Groq Investor Expects Half Her Bets To Fail
items.summary: Sandhya Venkatachalam spent the first half of her career building technology companies. She led product at an early data center hardware company that was sold to Cisco , then became a product executive at Skype before its sale to Microsoft . Those roles brought her into data and machine learning years before AI became venture capital’s dominant theme. She later became a general partner at Social Capital , where she led early institutional investments in AI chipmaker Groq , and later invested at Khosla Ventures . Now she’s founder and managing partner of Axiom Partners , a $52 million fund backing startups that use AI to do work in industries such as construction, industrials and insurance. In an interview with Crunchbase News, Venkatachalam discusses why she looks beyond familiar founder profiles, what makes an AI company durable, and how an early investment in Groq shaped her approach. This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity. Sandhya Venkatachalam, founder and managing partner of Axiom Partners. (Courtesy photo) You invested at Khosla Ventures before starting Axiom. What did you take from that experience, and what did you want to do differently? Venkatachalam: One thing I took was Vinod Khosla ’s open view of where great founders can come from. Silicon Valley has gravitated toward a fairly narrow idea of who can build the next great AI company: Someone with a Stanford computer science or machine learning background, or experience at OpenAI . We’re looking for more nonobvious founders, particularly in nonobvious industries. The other thing was how we think about risk. Instead of asking a company every conceivable diligence question, we focus on the risks that matter for its next set of milestones. Can this team do what it says it will do? And if it can, could the result be massive? That means accepting that many bets won’t work out while aiming for the outliers. I think that’s what my investors are backing me to do: identify categories of the future, rather than participate in the categories everyone already recognizes. At Axiom, the biggest difference is that we’ve built the firm around people who are actively working with AI. If you aren’t building, productizing, pricing or taking AI to market regularly, it’s very hard to keep up. Our team includes people doing exactly that in their other roles. They help keep our investment thinking current, and founders want to work with them because they’ve encountered many of the same challenges. We also use AI throughout the firm. We’ve built what we call the Axiom Brain to help us make sense of market trends, identify interesting people and companies, and move faster on diligence and other work. For me, the value is the ability to act quickly. You mentioned that some of those AI practitioners have other jobs. How does their role at Axiom work? Venkatachalam: They have dedicated time to Axiom and work with us part time. They also receive carry in the fund. They’re partners in the work, rather than people whose names appear on an adviser list. Their other jobs are central to the model. Some of the best angel investors are people who are still operating and building. I don’t need these people full time. In fact, they would be less valuable to Axiom if they left the work that keeps them close to the market. Axiom says it invests in “AI for the real world.” What does that mean when you’re evaluating a startup? Venkatachalam: Our view is that AI should benefit a much broader population than the early adopters who are already using it. We look at industries underserved by technology, where AI can produce an outcome rather than simply provide another software tool. That may lead us to construction, industrials or insurance. Some of those companies involve hardware, sensors or robotics; others are entirely software-based. What connects them is that they’re doing work that matters to customers in real-world industries. We generally don’t invest in products that look like conventional enterprise software tools. We want to see AI delivering a result. You’ve described a shift from software people use to digital workers that perform jobs. Are customers actually paying for AI from labor budgets? Venkatachalam: Yes, and that’s one of our investment criteria. Even when a portfolio company is at an alpha or design-partner stage, we do diligence to understand whether customers are willing to buy it that way. We’re often seeing contract values in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, rather than the much smaller contracts you might expect for a midmarket software tool. We’ve seen that buying behavior play out across the majority of the portfolio companies we’ve invested in. AI products are becoming faster to build and easier to imitate. What makes one durable enough to become a large company? Venkatachalam: If you’re doing important work inside a customer’s business, and that work is worth a lot of money, you become difficult to replace. You’re handling what we call the last mile of the job. In industrial settings, for example, delivering an outcome means integrating deeply with the systems customers use. You have to understand their data, train on it, learn the workflows that matter, and stand behind the result. That takes more than putting an interface on top of a model. Those relationships and capabilities can become difficult for another startup to replicate. They also involve work that the large AI model companies may have little interest in doing themselves. Before Axiom, you backed Groq when AI inference was far from an obvious investment category. What led you to it? Venkatachalam: I came from both hardware and software. At one point, I became interested in why Google was building its own networking switches when it could buy them from existing suppliers. As I looked into that, I learned it was building its own chips, too. That led me to Jonathan Ross , who had been involved in that work and had left to start Groq. I began learning why large technology companies were building chips to train models. Then Jonathan made the case that the much larger future market would be inference. I’ll be honest: In 2016, I barely understood inference. But if you believed these models would spread, it made sense that people would build on top of them and need the infrastructure to support that. That insight drove my investment. How did that experience shape what you look for now? Venkatachalam: It taught me the value of being a little early and having some patience. You don’t have to be wildly contrarian, but you do have to see the opportunity before it becomes obvious to everyone else. In a way, our thesis hasn’t changed. We’re still asking what will be built on top of AI infrastructure and models. We want to invest while the answer is emerging, before there’s a consensus. What happens when one of those early bets doesn’t work out? Venkatachalam: We plan for it. We have a $52 million fund and expect to make 35 investments. We fully expect about half of them to fail, whether that means a company shuts down or simply never reaches the growth trajectory we’re looking for. The model depends on finding an exceptional outcome. We need one outstanding investment to return the fund. If you invest early enough and the company becomes very large, that can offset many bets that didn’t work. That willingness to accept losses is part of making investments before an opportunity is obvious. It’s built into how we approach the fund. items.title: Generative AI Gives Spacecraft the Autonomy Engineers Once Feared
items.summary: Space was always supposed to be the final frontier of human exploration. It’s shaping up to be the final frontier for artificial intelligence too. Last December, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory used Anthropic’s Claude models to help plan two Mars drives for the Perseverance rover , with human planners checking and adjusting the route before upload. In May, NASA and IBM put a compressed AI model on the International Space Station and a satellite to identify things like floods and clouds from orbit, the first model of its kind demonstrated in space. And in July, astronauts on the ISStested out a large language model to see if it could help with questions on maintenance procedures . These experiments point to a larger shift in space engineering. For decades, engineers on Earth determined what a machine in space would do, and the machine would do exactly that. Now, researchers are testing whether non-deterministic systems like generative AI can give spacecraft more flexibility to interpret their surroundings, plan tasks, and one day make decisions for themselves. The technology is still far from trustworthy enough to hand over control of a spacecraft, but engineers are starting to ask whether they can afford not to as missions become more complex, distant, and numerous. Why Spacecraft Need True Autonomy Spacecraft have been operating autonomously for decades. But autonomy has never been the dominant model, in part because space engineers have prized systems whose behavior they can predict. “Autonomy often does not have a deterministic outcome, which means that how you got into a certain situation changes the behavior,” says Robert Ambrose , the former chief of NASA’s Software, Robotics and Simulation Division . “So if you come into the same situation but from different paths, the outcome could be different. And so engineers hate that.” Ambrose spent much of his career working on autonomous systems at NASA, including autonomy for the Orion spacecraft , NASA’s deep space and lunar orbiter spacecraft, and Robonaut 2 , a humanoid robot designed to work alongside astronauts and went to space in 2011. With Orion, he saw how quickly the testing problem could multiply. Engineers had to consider not just what the spacecraft might do, but all the different ways it could have arrived at a decision. But Ambrose says engineers found ways to manage that complexity, including automating the testing itself. “We fought the challenges of autonomy using autonomy,” he says. “That actually works.” The need for autonomy becomes even more obvious the farther a mission travels from Earth. Ambrose points to a possible mission to Europa, Jupiter’s ice-crusted moon, where a spacecraft could dive through a water plume erupting from beneath the surface. The plume could appear too quickly for engineers on Earth to direct the spacecraft into it. “It’s up to the spacecraft to make a decision, and we’ll be watching what happened an hour ago,” he says. A mission like that, he added, is “totally impossible” without giving the machine real autonomy. Icarus Robotics engineers gather valuable training data for a free-flying robotic system—destined for the International Space Station—during a zero-G flight. Icarus Robotics Adapting Robotics to Microgravity Physics As AI and robotics advance on Earth, a commercial space boom is creating new opportunities to put those technologies to work in orbit. But what works on Earth does not necessarily work in space. Icarus Robotics is developing what it calls a robotic labor force for space. This includes Joy, a free-flying robotic system. Joy recently finished zero-gravity testing in Canada ahead of a planned deployment to the ISS, where one of its first tasks would be moving cargo bags between modules. The company plans to start with teleoperation, using that data to eventually train the robots to work on their own. “What the rollout will probably look like is something much closer to beginning with partial autonomy, so you still have human supervision in the loop at all times,” says Jamie Palmer , Icarus’s co-founder and CTO. A robot trained on Earth learns from the physics of the environment around it, Palmer says, and in orbit, the physics is entirely different. “If you take the newest Gemini robotics model, or you take the newest physical intelligence model, and you put it in zero-G there, it’s just going to fail immediately,” he says. On Earth, for example, a robot learns that when it pushes something off a table, the object falls. In orbit, it keeps moving. That leaves Icarus with a problem the terrestrial robotics industry also faces, but in a more extreme form: There is very little real-world data from the environment where its robots will operate. The company is combining demonstrations from its robots in microgravity with simulations and tests on Earth to build its own dataset. “I wish there was” an available dataset Icarus could download and use, says Ethan Barajas , the company’s co-founder and CEO. “But there’s not today, not in a meaningful way.” Managing Autonomous Spacecraft Risk The challenge is not simply teaching spacecraft to act on their own. It is figuring out how to manage the risks of giving them more freedom. “It has been mind-boggling to me how little autonomy we have in space applications,” says Ufuk Topcu , an engineering professor at The University of Texas at Austin and the director of the Center for Autonomy. “Because it’s exactly the place where human involvement is extremely hard, the stakes are high, and you need to act fast.” Topcu says that the goal cannot be to guarantee that autonomous systems will never do anything wrong. They’re most useful in situations humans cannot anticipate, he says, so instead researchers need to start with restricted applications, learn how the systems behave, and gradually expand where and how they are used. The real question, in his view, is how well the risk of deployment is managed, not whether they can be fully eliminated. That may become increasingly important as the space industry changes. For most of the space age, a small number of government agencies designed missions that could take decades to develop and operate. Commercial companies are now putting more spacecraft into orbit, and new missions can be developed and launched much faster. “Space used to have very slow innovation cycles,” Topcu says. “They would think of a mission concept and spend 10 or 15 years on it. It’s not like that anymore. Everything is evolving faster now.”

Icarus Robotics engineers gather valuable training data for a free-flying robotic system—destined for the International Space Station—during a zero-G flight.Icarus Robotics

Adapting Robotics to Microgravity Physics

As AI and robotics advance on Earth, a commercial space boom is creating new opportunities to put those technologies to work in orbit. But what works on Earth does not necessarily work in space.

Icarus Robotics is developing what it calls a robotic labor force for space. This includes Joy, a free-flying robotic system. Joy recently finished zero-gravity testing in Canada ahead of a planned deployment to the ISS, where one of its first tasks would be moving cargo bags between modules. The company plans to start with teleoperation, using that data to eventually train the robots to work on their own.

“What the rollout will probably look like is something much closer to beginning with partial autonomy, so you still have human supervision in the loop at all times,” says Jamie Palmer, Icarus’s co-founder and CTO.

A robot trained on Earth learns from the physics of the environment around it, Palmer says, and in orbit, the physics is entirely different.

“If you take the newest Gemini robotics model, or you take the newest physical intelligence model, and you put it in zero-G there, it’s just going to fail immediately,” he says. On Earth, for example, a robot learns that when it pushes something off a table, the object falls. In orbit, it keeps moving.

That leaves Icarus with a problem the terrestrial robotics industry also faces, but in a more extreme form: There is very little real-world data from the environment where its robots will operate. The company is combining demonstrations from its robots in microgravity with simulations and tests on Earth to build its own dataset. “I wish there was” an available dataset Icarus could download and use, says Ethan Barajas, the company’s co-founder and CEO. “But there’s not today, not in a meaningful way.”

Managing Autonomous Spacecraft Risk

The challenge is not simply teaching spacecraft to act on their own. It is figuring out how to manage the risks of giving them more freedom.

“It has been mind-boggling to me how little autonomy we have in space applications,” says Ufuk Topcu, an engineering professor at The University of Texas at Austin and the director of the Center for Autonomy. “Because it’s exactly the place where human involvement is extremely hard, the stakes are high, and you need to act fast.”

Topcu says that the goal cannot be to guarantee that autonomous systems will never do anything wrong. They’re most useful in situations humans cannot anticipate, he says, so instead researchers need to start with restricted applications, learn how the systems behave, and gradually expand where and how they are used. The real question, in his view, is how well the risk of deployment is managed, not whether they can be fully eliminated.

That may become increasingly important as the space industry changes. For most of the space age, a small number of government agencies designed missions that could take decades to develop and operate. Commercial companies are now putting more spacecraft into orbit, and new missions can be developed and launched much faster.

“Space used to have very slow innovation cycles,” Topcu says. “They would think of a mission concept and spend 10 or 15 years on it. It’s not like that anymore. Everything is evolving faster now.”

items.title: I asked Instinct to plan 2 trips for me — and it sucked all the joy out of traveling
items.summary: I felt much more excited planning a vacation to Amsterdam myself than when the agent took nearly an hour figuring it out. Andrey Danilovich/Getty Images I used Instinct's AI agent to plan a work trip and a European vacation. For the work trip, it quickly created a solid itinerary but suggested an impossible flight. When I asked for help with a vacation, it took much longer and sucked out the excitement of travel. Ask around: AI agents are the Next Big Thing. You can give them tasks via iMessage or WhatsApp, and they can search the internet or use software to complete them. It's a bit like having a concierge or assistant who can book restaurants or reply to emails for you. When I used one to plan a trip , I was underwhelmed to say the least. In fact, it had me questioning the point of travel. Is it to check another country off your list and follow a set itinerary, or to explore somewhere new and connect with different people? I put two scenarios to the test: a business trip and a European city break . The agent was far more useful for the former, but it still slipped up with a pretty obvious mistake. I live in London, and since Meta's Muse isn't yet available outside the US, I asked a colleague for an invite to use Instinct's AI agent . I decided on a hypothetical three-night trip to Business Insider's headquarters in New York. I would check a bag and avoid flying overnight (sleeping on an airplane is a tantalizing, if impossible, goal for me). First, I picked the dates and planned the trip out myself. After half an hour on Google Flights and Booking.com — plus checking public transit costs and the company policy on meal expenses — I had a rudimentary document calculating a roughly $2,000 budget. Instinct only took about 10 minutes to create a four-page doc replete with details. Each section included a paragraph explaining its reasoning, a brief schedule, and links to sources at the end. However, the agent committed a basic error with the flights. It suggested I fly from London to New York with Delta Air Lines, but return with British Airways to avoid a red-eye. It's impossible to book these two airlines on the same ticket — the sort of thing that's obvious when you're researching flights yourself. Pete Syme/Business Insider Instinct took six minutes to rectify the mistake and update the doc with a daytime return flight on Virgin Atlantic for about $130 extra. (Delta has a 49% stake in Virgin Atlantic, so flights with either airline can be booked through the other.) So, in the end, our budgets were the same, but Instinct created a more thorough plan in half the time. It also probably could've figured out the flight issue itself if I had prompted it to actually book the trip. I therefore had fairly high hopes when it came to planning a weekend vacation. Instead, it ended up feeling a bit pointless. In this instance, the criteria were broader because I wanted to explore my options. I was in the mood to visit a European city with a top art gallery sometime in November, and maybe take a Eurostar train if the price was right. It took me about 20 minutes to decide on Amsterdam, one of five direct Eurostar destinations from London, with a vast number of artworks at both the Rijksmuseum and the Van Gogh Museum. When I prompted Instinct, it ended up taking a lot longer than I expected. My enthusiasm waned. Visions of sunflowers and canals became distant memories as boredom took hold. Perhaps I'm exaggerating slightly, but it still got me thinking: What is the point of handing this over to an AI agent if it flattens my excitement to travel? Instinct replied after half an hour with a list of five cities and approximate budgets. It suggested I narrow its list down to two cities, then took another 23 minutes to come up with specific dates, hotels, and transport options. Pete Syme/Business Insider During that time, ChatGPT gave me a similar list in three minutes. I also spent some more time exploring the cost of going to Vienna or Copenhagen. Instinct's most useful feature was giving it the measurements of my carry-on so it could account for extra fees charged by some airlines, saving me from having to investigate all the different terms. However, it suggested an Amsterdam hotel that I didn't love the look of, with cramped, tacky rooms. Plus, its Eurostar pricing was about $30 more than what I found on the company's website, which helpfully shows the cheapest options across a month. Ultimately, giving an AI agent broad guidelines to suggest vacation ideas isn't the best use of its capabilities. Although a chatbot was quicker, it still sucked away the fun of perusing different options and picturing what the ideal trip could look like. Chatting to the agent via WhatsApp also felt a bit uncanny, as if it was trying to resemble a real conversation without the humanity. For example, the way it splits its points into different messages is like you might when texting a friend. I was a bit irritated when my phone pinged four times, including the agent changing its emoji reaction to a checkbox after completing the task. Ultimately, I think it's pretty nifty for planning travel that you're not too bothered about, like a business trip that requires precise costs and a corporate budget. There's still the caveat that, as with all AI tools, double-checking is imperative. If you're looking for travel inspiration, though, chatbots are likely more useful. Even if you're pressed for time and racing to check another destination off your bucket list , isn't it more thrilling to press the book button yourself? Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Apple’s long, lonely game in the AR race
items.summary: Meta’s most recent product announcements have grabbed attention, but the one thing they could not hide is that it’s still not possible to build a system as sophisticated as Apple’s Vision Pro at an affordable price, or Meta would have done it. You could argue that at $1,299, the Meta VR Glasses the company introduced last week and promised to ship in spring 2027 could be as sophisticated, but they do betray some significant design compromises that Apple seems to have avoided. The most glaring compromise is the use of a puck to carry the processor and battery, so the glasses weigh just 100 grams. Even now, a recent Bloomberg report tells us that senior Apple decision makers have resisted use of an external puck to help reduce the weight and cost of future Vision Pro models, holding steady to the fully integrated device model typical of Apple’s products. (While Apple will have its reasons, I’m not certain that’s the correct approach, as the company could effectively sell two products, the headset and the puck, making both systems available on a biennial upgrade.) There are other compromises as well — for example, Meta’s glasses seem to deliver a narrower field of view than the current Vision Pro. At the same time, the competition between the two firms hints at the technological barriers Apple is trying to solve. After all this time since the introduction of the first Vision Pro , Meta still can’t match the field of view, and even with a puck rather than an integrated build, its alternative still costs a fair bit of cash, while the processor it plans to power the glasses with isn’t even available yet. Think about that. It means Meta and its partners are still building a processor with which to match Apple’s. If that’s not a technical challenge, I don’t know what is. The roadmap for visionOS This isn’t about Meta bashing or Apple building. It’s about how Apple has always openly described Vision Pro as a product from the future. Even earlier this month, CEO John Ternus said , “I think of it [Vision Pro] as like the early days of computers. It is the early days of a long journey. That’s how I feel about Vision Pro.” Meta’s new product and the latest reports from inside Apple show that the future takes time to build. On the journey to doing so, the company now seems to be contemplating four potential paths: A Vision Pro design using lighter, potentially lower-cost materials such as plastic or titanium. A design that offloads components to a puck. Smart glasses with audio, camera, and AI, which Apple hopes to introduce by the end of 2027. Smart glasses with audio, camera, AI, and a video display, which feels like the most appropriate endgame for both Vision Pro and smart glasses products. I don’t think the consequences of taking any of those paths should be seen as zero-sum options, but as priorities toward an eventual goal for pervasive spatial computing, combining always-aware contextual AI with wearable computing designed to deliver powerful augmentation across all parts of life. The Bloomberg report suggests that Apple is in a state of flux regarding its next move with Vision Pro, complete with a reference to the work being on “life support.” I’d argue that Apple is in the lull before the spatial storm . What happens next is under review. What amazing timing However, this must be contextualized against the depth of competition between Apple and Meta. The timing of these claims — coming so soon after Meta’s latest product reveal — is a gift to Meta’s marketing machine. At Apple’s scale, it is entirely possible to pursue multiple parallel designs, so any perceived internal confusion may simply reflect different degrees of preparedness across all four (and possibly more) of these projects. Management may simply have been waiting to see what Meta did before accelerating any of these initiatives. While there have allegedly been some recent redundancies in the Vision Pro team, Apple’s new leader doesn’t seem to have gone cold on the product. It’s more as if he accepts that Apple is in it for the long haul. A long-haul destination That long-term commitment allows Apple time to refine key components of its product plans, particularly around privacy . Apple wants to avoid the stigma of “ pervert glasses ,” which is why its work on ambient audio intelligence requires close scrutiny. The decisions it takes to protect privacy there — including use of Secure Exclave — will I believe be emulated across the future visionOS product range. In the short term, the most telling insights we’ll see will be the pushback Apple and Meta face from global privacy regulators, for AR in Meta’s case, and for Audio Intelligence in the case of Apple. Those decisions will set the framework both for Apple’s future AR products and the future of consumer/enterprise mass-market AR. Now please subscribe to my daily, human-curated Apple-related news headline feed at The Core , or follow me on BlueSky , LinkedIn , or Mastodon . < > >> >> >> >> >

You could argue that at $1,299, the Meta VR Glasses the company introduced last week and promised to ship in spring 2027 could be as sophisticated, but they do betray some significant design compromises that Apple seems to have avoided. 

The most glaring compromise is the use of a puck to carry the processor and battery, so the glasses weigh just 100 grams. Even now, a recent Bloomberg report tells us that senior Apple decision makers have resisted use of an external puck to help reduce the weight and cost of future Vision Pro models, holding steady to the fully integrated device model typical of Apple’s products.
